STAPLES (Macdonald) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 146) to amend the Interest Act. He said:	The
object of this Bill is to remedy certain grievances which at present exist, more particularly in the western provinces, where there is a great deal of buying and selling of land. For instance, if a farmer wishes to increase the amount of a loan on his land, he is at the mercy of the company which has made the existing loan, and if he desires to pay off the loan, he has to pay the bonus stipulated in the mortgage, which is sometimes very excessive. This measure is proposed for the purpose of remedying these grievances, and making it easier to conduct business in the buying and selling of land in the west.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Before the Orders of the Day are taken up, I notice that a good deal of interest is being exhibited at the present time in the suggestion of Sir Edward Grey as to the desirability and the possibility of obtaining an arbitration treaty between England and the United States. As this would appear to be a matter of very great and far-reaching importance, in which I have no doubt Canada as well as the mother country and the United States is interested, equally with all other civilized countries in the world, I would like to ask the government if they have had any communication with the Imperial government or with the United States government on this subject, and if so, if they have anything which they can communicate to the House and through the House to the country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The government has received no communication whatever, either from the Imperial authorities or from the United States on this very important subject; but I have no hesitation in adding that if it were in the power of Canada in any way to help towards such a laudable object, we would be only too glad to do so.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday last I asked the Prime Minister a question which you, Sir, cut off, so that he could not answer. It was in connection with a matter brought up by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell), that is, a speech made by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), in regard to which the Prime Minister said:
The statement made by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) was quite consistent with our policy, it was nothing new, and he had perfect authority, not only he but every member of the Liberal side, to make that statement.
I asked the right hon. the Prime Minister, what I would like to repeat now, whether his remarks also applied to the British preference?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

If I understood correctly the Prime Minister's statement in reply to the hon. member for Dauphin, it was that every Liberal member had the liberty of making the statement, it being the policy of the government. Would not the members of the opposition have the same liberty?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the patience of the House for a few moments on a question of privilege. In a somewhat heated incident which occurred in the House on Friday afternoon, of whieh the member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) and myself were among the chief actors, a statement was made by the member for Dauphin which I did not catch at the time, but which I find reported in the public press of the country, and also in the Unrevised ' Hansard. As this statement, or insinuation, contained in a certain question asked by the member for Dauphin, reflects very seriously on my honour as a member of this House, and has been sent broadcast throughout the country, I think it only fair that it should be taken into consideration. On page 5669 of ' Hansard ' appears the following statement:

He had better talk of his honesty? Where is the capital of Saskatchewan? What does it cost to vote for it?
And on the next page the member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes), referring to some remarks which I had made in reference to the member for Dauphin, made this statement:
Did he sell the capital of Saskatchewan?
At the moment there was so much confusion in the House that I did not catch the words of the member for Dauphin, and I did not know that he had made use of such words until I saw them in the columns of the public press on the following day. I did catch the word ' honesty ' but the rest of the statement I did not catch; and as it reflects very seriously upon me, as a member of this House, I rise to a question of personal explanation and privilege. If the House will pardon me a moment, I should find it necessary to explain,to some

extent what my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) referred to. As many hon. members know, it was my good or ill fortune to be a member of the first legislature of the province of Saskatchewan; and one of the .first important questions that came before that legislature was the question of the location of the capital. It so happened that the majority of the supporters of the government of that province came from the northern part of Saskatchewan; and in the west it is well known that the two chief competitors or rivals for the honour of being the capital were the cities of Saskatoon in the north and Regina in the south. I am free to say that, on the part of many of us, our personal inclinations were in favour of Saskatoon; but when we came to Regina and the question came to be decided, we discovered that the government intended to deal with it as a government mdbsure and had decided to make the capital where it had been for many years, in the old city of Regina. Some of us had even gone so far as to express publicly I was not one of them-our preference for the selection of Saskatoon, but as the government had made the choice of Regina a government measure, we decided to support the government rather than insist on our personal preference, and I personally have no regret for the action I then took. In the debate in the provincial legislature a certain member of the opposition twitted government supporters with having supported the government measure against their own sentiment and suggested that coercion had been used by the First Minister of Saskatchewan in order to compel them to do so. He also went so far as to make the insinuation that possibly the first minister, or some one on his behalf, had used other means to induce his followers to support it. But upon being challenged by the first minister to make good his insinuation, he refused to make any charge against any supporter of the government and the incident closed so far as the House was concerned and no reference was made to it afterwards. The opposition press of the province, however, took up the insinuation and published it broadcast. That insinuation was to the effect that the government of Saskatchewan or its prime minister, or some one on his behalf, had used other means than persuasion to influence certain members to support the government in its location of the capital. In the general election which followed, these insinuations were not believed by the people, and the men who were subjected to them were returned to' parliament. It would appear that a lie has sometimes a long life, and these slanderous insinuations were again brought to life in the debate on Friday last by the hon. members for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) and Dauphin (Mr. Campbell). It has been my
privilege to serve the constituency of Humboldt not only in this House, the short time I have been here, but during the first term of the legislature ui Saskatchewan, and I want to say to my hon. friend from Dauphin (Mr. Campbell), who has repeated the insinuation, that, so far as I am personally concerned, if he can adduce one particle of proof that, in my public capacity as a representative of the constituency of Humboldt, either in the local legislature or this House, I have ever done anything or cast a single vote for financial reward or hope of financial reward or from any other motive than a sense of public duty, I shall forfeit my seat in this House. I want to go further and say that if, as the representative of the people, he can find one single instance in which I have rendered a service to a constituent of mine, as a public man, for financial reward or hope of financial reward, my seat its vacant in this House. I did make a certain statement with reference to the hon. member for Dauphin on Friday last, which he denied. That statement was that he had said a certain thing in the last local election in the province of Manitoba. He denied having made that statement and I accepted hiiis denial. I accepted it as an acceptance due from one hon. member to another. And to-day I appeal to the hon. gentleman, as an appeal from man to man, that he should either withdraw the insinuation he made or let me know-and I think it is only fair that I should know- what foundation he had for making it. As I have done him the credit of accepting his denial, just as I would accept the statement of any member of this House, I appeal to him either to accept the denial that I make of the insinuation he cast upon me or furnish some proof of it.

I have listened very carefully to what has been said by the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely). There is no man in this House who regrets an incident such as that which occurred on Friday night more than I do. But while I say that, I wish the House to understand that I do not consider myself in the least degree responsible. We all regret instances of that kind. We all at times, under provocation, are apt to forget what is due from one to the other, and are apt to make statements off the bat which are perhaps too emphatic and not capable perhaps of being proven to our satisfaction. The speech just made by my hon. friend from Humboldt gives the answer to the question that he propounded to me. What I said on the floor of this House contained no specific charge against the hon. member, but of course he is at liberty to put on it what interpretation he chooses. He has himself admitted-and I do not propose to

adduce any other evidence than what he has himself given with regard to the innuendo-that it was stated on the floor of the Saskatchewan legislature that other means had been used to persuade members from the north of the province to vote foT the choice of Regina as a location for the capital of that province instead of Saskatoon. That was my authority for making the remarks I did. It was stated, under flaring headlines, in the newspapers in the northwest, that some influences had been brought to bear, not party or political influences, but others, to induce members to deviate from their loyalty to the town in their own part of the country, Saskatoon, to which they were pledged to give their support in the question of whether Regina or Saskatoon should-
The hon. gentleman (Mt. Campbell) is wrong. No man was- pledged.

What pledges a man,. Mr. Speaker? Is a promise given to a friend not a pledge? I leave it to ' Hansard ' to say whether the hon. member (Mr. Neely), in his remarks a few'anomemts ago^ did not state that some had made a pTo-mise to their friends, and, for my part, I consider a promise made is a debt unpaid.
I did not say anything of the kind; I said they had expressed sentiments in favour.

I was careful not to interrupt the hon. .member when he was speaking. I have the desire that every member of this House has, to have every member, regardless of his party politics, appear at his best; and that is the reason I did not interrupt him. But we have from him now an interruption of my words. I do not desire this House to ask for me, and I do not intend to give them, an interpretation of my words. I am quite willing to accept the interpretation put upon my words by the hon. member for Humboldt. At the same time, I want to tell him, when he gets up in this House and sayis that the facts of the case do not bear out the interpretation that he himself put on my words, I aim quite willing, as a member of this House, to- accept his word frankly and freely. I think that thiat is all that is necessary to settle the matter.

It is not often that I rise in this House to a question of privilege,- I do not know that I ever have done it before. I would wait for the motion which is expected within' a short time to bring forward the matter to which I wish to speak, but, as I have to refer to a past debate, I might be ruled out of order. The Mr. CAMPBELL.
hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) on Thursday last, as will be seen by referring to page 5584 of ' Hansard,' speaking when I was not in the House, spoke of a matter that had taken place in the Customs. I have the return before me, but if bon. members will refer to ' Hansard,' they can trace the whole transaction showing that it was carried out in the ordinary course of the business of the department. Yet it was placed before this House in a light that is unfair,-I need not use a -stronger word-unjust, very unfair and veTy unjust, to the officers of my department. I, therefore, on their behalf, wish to bring the matter before the House. The case referred to was that of a yacht that had been bought by Mr. Travers-or, rather, not bought, but received by him as a gift, and, as a gift, of course,,-unaccompanied by an invoice. The usual course was followed. There had to be a valuation by one of our -appraisers -duly qualified for that purpose and that was dome. Mr. Travers wrote to Mr. Calvert to ask him if he would bring the matter before the commissioner. He had a conversation with the commissioner, and, subsequently, be wrote a letter to the commissioner. I will not take up the -time of the House by reading the whole correspondence, -as it is given in ' Hansard,' at the page already referred to, but I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite, as well as hon. members on this side, to go- through the whole matter so that they may see how very, very unfair and unjust the hon. gentleman was in -the remarks he made at that time and -the conclusions he sought to draw from th-e facts he gave. This was am ordinary transaction. The hon. member (Mr. Sharpe, Ontario) makes the point: Why did not Mr. T-ravers write to the Customs Department himself? Why did he ask Mr. Calvert, the Liberal -whip, to do it? There is not a week passes but members of piarliament bring matters- before my department with reference to their constituents, and sometimes with reference to those who -are not their constituents. The hon. member (Mr. Sharpe, Ontario) is surrounded by those who have done the same thing. They bring these matters to our department, and they are examined into, their representations are heard, and then the department does w-hat it considers to be right in th-e matter. That was wh-aft was done, and that is- -all that was done in this case. The hon. gentleman from North Ontario omitted reading the letter from Mr. Travers to Mr. Calvert in which he asked Mr. Calvert to have the departmental machinery to he used in making valuations put in motion, -at least that letter is not in ' Hansard.'
Was that letter in the return brought down?
I think it was. It is1 in the papers before me which purport to be a copy of that return.
I think I read the whole correspondence.

I refer hon. members' to show that that letter is not there. The hon. member (Mr. Sharpe, Ontario) said:
Not only did Mr. Calvert exercise his influence with the Einance Department in connection with the passing of this certificate through the Treasury Board, but he exercised his influence with the Customs Department on behalf of Mr. Travers. I moved for a return the other day in connection with a pleasure yacht which Travers had transferred from the register at Detroit to Brockville. Mr. Calvert seems to have been under some obligation and Mr. Travers wrote to him, August 18, 1909, just when everybody was clamouring for an investigation, when the insurance department of New York State was asking for an investigation into the affairs of the bank. Mr. Travers was doing everything he could to stave off that investigation. Instead of writing direct to the Customs Department we find him writing to Mr. Calvert as follows:
Then, after reading that letter, the hon. gentleman comments as follows:
That is about a month after the loan to Mr. Calvert. Travers writes to him asking him to get his boat passed at a low valuation. Mr. Calvert writes to Mr. McDougald, Commissioner of Customs, on the 19th of August, after having a personal conversation with that gentleman. His letter reads:
Then he Teads the letter sent by Mr. Calvert and comments further in the following words:
So you see Mr. Calvert, the Liberal whip, had personally interviewed the Commissioner of Customs with a view to getting the boat through the Customs at a low valuation, and actually suggested the valuation. If the Minister of Customs were here I would ask if that is the way the Customs Department is managed. This transaction came to light by accident, and I would ask how many entries are made through the Customs Department on the advice of the Liberal whip. It is an extraordinary circumstance and the Prime Minister should take cognizance of the matter.
It was not necessary to appeal to the Prime Minister to take cognizance of a matter passing in the Customs Department. Any charges made or insinuations thrown out the minister of the department is quite competent and willing to deal with.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Paterson) was not in his place. That was the reason I appealed to the Prime Minister.

It was not necessary to appeal to the Prime Minister. The matter came to my notice the next morning in a paragraph in the newspaper. I was
asked if I had seen the very extraordinary charge made-very unjust.

I rise to a point of order. When an hon. member rises to a question of privilege, is he not confined to a personal explanation? I do not think he has the right to use a question of privilege to make an attack on another member of the House. I want an opportunity to reply, to justify what I have said.
The hon. gentleman will have an opportunity.
The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) has sat long enough in this House to know the custom of the House in relation ito questions of privilege I assume that he will observe the Tules of the House.

Certainly. As I explained, had it not been that it was necessary for me to refer to a past debate, I should have waited for the motion that is soon to be presented to the House. Then he reads another letter. Then we have a letter from Mr. Farrow. The commissioner wrote that the only way to have a waluation of the boat made would be for one of our special officers, appointed as an appraiser, whose duty it is to make valuations in all parts of the west of machinery to go there and make an examination. I have to ask my hon. friend a question. He says the boat was valued at $1,600, by our Dominion appraiser Mr. Boughney. I have here a communication from the collector of customs at Brockville, whose duty it would have been in the absence of the special appraiser to make this appraisement. The collector at Brockville says that he was aware of the valuation, that he approved of it, and that the boat was not worth any more. The hon. member says:
The valuation is interesting. I am informed that the boilers and engine alone for scrap iron would be worth several thousand dollars. It is a most expensive yacht, and it is valued on the suggestion of Mr. Calvert at the low sum of $1,600. Mr. Calvert suggested $1,000 or so,

And that is not an ingenuous statement.
-and the Customs Department being in an accommodating mood split the difference and made it $1,600. That matter should be taken cognizance of by the leader of the government. Mr. Calvert had been the instrument in securing the passing of the Farmers' Bank certificate; he was the instrument in having the yacht 'Wanda' passed the customs at on&-twentieth of its true value. Why did not Mr. Travers deal direct with the Customs Department instead of using the Liberal whip to secure the valuation of a boat worth thousands and thousands of dollars at $1,600. The Customs Department through the influence of the Liberal whip was defrauded out of hundreds of dollars in duty.

One of my deputies has sent me the following extract, within the last two or three minutes:
The former Literal Whip, Mr. W. S. Calvert, now a member of the Transcontinental Railway Commission, had introduced Mr. Travers to the Minister of Finance. He had also used his influence with Hon. Wm. Paterson, Minister of Customs, to have Mr. Travers' yacht 'Wanda' passed through the customs at the low valuation of $1,600.
I need scarcely say that I knew nothing of the transaction whatever as my officer writes me. He says:
Hear Mr. Paterson,-I wish to call your attention to above quoted extract from the 'Mail and Empire' of Friday last re Travers' yacht.
Yours respectfully,

I find from reference to correspondence that you were not in Ottawa until the 26th August 1909, upon which date you returned to the city. Departmental letters re yacht are dated 24th August, 1909.
Of course I have not to deal with this comment from a newspaper. This paper has often in the past and will probably in the future make comments which woulA not be called complimentary to me, and which in this case are absolutely unjust, but I have to do with an hon. member of this House making charges so serious as this which involves the reputation, and as you can see, absolutely the position of an officer of the Department of Customs. _ The hon. member says he does that on _ information. The officer cannot question a member of parliament whose statement is privileged, but I have a Tight to ask, and I do ask on behalf of my officer that that hon. gentleman be just enough to these men to give me the name of his informant. Then we will trace it out. It needs no royal commission, it will be attended to, but I ask him and I think the House will agree with me that in justice to these men if not to myself he should give the name of this informant who can be talked to outside of the House.
Would the minister give us the particulars of the yacht, her size, dimensions and engines?

If the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) gives _ the name of his informant will the minister deal with him as diligently and expeditiously as he did with those officers of the Customs Department in Cape Breton who broke the regulations of the Customs Department by taking part in municipal elections and which I have brought to his attention time and time again?

In reply to the leader of the opposition this memorandum is handed to me signed by John McDougald, Mr. PATERSON.
commissioner of customs and R. R. Farrow, assistant commissioner. An insinuation was made because Mr. McDougald was addressed by Mr. Calvert and the letter was written by Mr. Farrow. I am informed that Mr. McDougald had gone on his holidays and in the regular course of correspondence the letter came to Mr. Farrow and he answered it. The memorandum which has been handed to me reads:
This appraisement was made by J. C. Boughner in the usual course.
Mr. Boughner is a Dominion appraiser appointed under the Customs Act especially for appraisement of machinery, for which purpose he visits from time to time ports in eastern Canada where there are no regular appraisers.
There is no appraiser at Brockville. The collector acts there as appraising officer in the absence of a regular appraiser.
In this instance, Mr. Boughner conferred with the collector in making the appraisement. The collector states that he considers the appraisement of $1,600 a proper valuation, and that the vessel is not worth any more.
Mr. Boughner received no instructions whatever, directly or indirectly, from the officers of the Customs Department as to making a low appraisement.	_
There was no invoice, and the valuation was left to the appraiser's judgment. He maintains that his appraisement was fair and reasonable.
The yacht is 25 tons gross register, 17 tons net register; built of wood in 1892; with steam engines of 13 horse power. At the time of appraisement in 1909 the hull and engines were 17 years old; boilers 14 years old.

Any person who listened to my remarks the other night would know I was not reflecting at all upon the personal integrity_of the Minister of Customs. Every one who has the acquaintance of the Minister of Customs knows perfectly well that he would not be a party to this, but I do reflect upon, his department, and until there is an investigation granted, that reflection stands. My information, and I have it from a good source, which I am willing to disclose at a proper investigation
No, but I want it now.

And if the minister will grant a royal commission to investigate this I will disclose the names and circumstances connected with the whole discreditable transaction. In my opinion the whole affair shows a most improper and discreditable state of affairs in the Department of Customs, and I am willing to stand by what I said, and to give the information in detail if a royal commission is granted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to observe that my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) does not impute any wrong action to the

minister, who3e perfect integrity he acknowledges. He says that if anything wrong has been done it has been on the part of the officers of the department, Mr. Mc-Dougald to whom Mr. Calvert's communication was addressed, or Mr. Farrow. All the members who were in the House years ago, and hon. gentlemen who have been in the House for some time know that while the government is blessed with a very good civil service the government has no better officers than Mr. McDougald and Mr. Farrow and that their integrity is absolutely above reproach.

The position of the appraiser is at stake on this point. He has taken an oath to do his duty. He is charged with having placed a valuation upon a boat which is one-twentieth its value. The hon. gentleman says that he has information to that effect. I say that this officer has the right, through me, to say to the hon. gentleman who makes this statement that he must give the name of the informant, and give it now if he wishes to be fair.

In reply to the Minister of Customs, I know of no authority which says that I must give it now, and I shall refuse to give it now. I will give it at any proper session of a royal commission that may be appointed to investigate this whole transaction.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that, whereas by legislation enacted at the session thereof held in the year A.D. 1910, the legislature of the province of New Brunswick authorized and empowered the Lieutenant Governor in Council for the said province to guarantee the principal and interest of the bonds of any railway company which would build a line of railway from a point on the line of the National Transcontinental railway at Grand Falls, in the county of Victoria, to the city of St. John, in the said province of New Brunswick, a distance of about two hundred and twenty miles, to the extent of twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000) per mile upon certain conditions therein set forth, one of such conditions being that no such agreement should be entered into with any company or corporation for the construction of the said line of railway or for the guaranteeing of the said bonds unless and until the parliament of Canada should enact legislation authorizing the entering by the government of Canada into an agreement with such company or with the government of the province of New Brunswick, for the leasing of the said line of railway when completed, with its appurtenances and rolling stock, and for the operation, maintenance, upkeep and repair by the said government of Canada, as a part of the government railway system of Canada, for a period of ninety-nine years, and for the payment by the government of Canada to the said province of New Brunswick, or the government thereof, each year during the said term of ninety-nine years of forty per centum per annum of the gross earnings of the said railway, as or in the nature of rental therefor; the amount of such

rental to be applied in payment of the interest of the bonds so to be guaranteed and the surplus, if any, to be paid to the said company.
Now, therefore, it is expedient that His Excellency the Governor in Council be authorized to enter into a contract with any such railroad company and the government of the province of New Brunswick as aforesaid, for the leasing of the said line of railway with its appurtenances and rolling stock, when completed and equipped with rolling stock, and for the operation, maintenance, upkeep and repair by the said government of Canada, as a part of the government railway system of Canada, for a period of ninety-nine years, and for the payment by the government of Canada to the said province of New Brunswick, or the said company, each year during the said term of ninety-nine years, of the forty per centum per annum of the gross earnings of the said railway, as or in the nature of rental therefor;
Provided, however, that the said contract shall be entered into only upon the condition that the said railway be constructed upon plans and specifications to be approved of by the Governor in Council upon the recommendation of the Minister of Railways and Canals, and shall be up to the general standard of the said National Transcontinental railway through the said province;
Provided further, that His Excellency the Governor in Council shall be authorized to enter into a contract as aforesaid for the operation of the said road in sections, when completed and equipped as follows:
1.	Prom Predericton to Woodstock.
2.	Prom Fredericton south a distance of fifty miles.
3.	Each twenty-five miles thereafter, until the line be completed and equipped from Grand Falls to St. John.-Mr. Graham.

This resolution refers to a proposed line of railway 207 miles long running from the city of St. John to Grand Falls. I may say that one of the first deputations that I listened to after becoming a member of the government was a large deputation from this part of the Dominion urging that steps be taken to secure the construction of a line of railway through the rich St. John valley. If I remember correctly, what was promised at that date was the granting of the usual subsidy, which I think was done at the following session of parliament. Although this is one of the oldest sections of the Dominion, and said to be one of the richest, it seems to have had difficulty in getting railway facilities. Several attempts have been made, but they have not hitherto been brought to a successful conclusion. So urgent is the necessity for this line, and so much has its need impressed the minds of legislators, both in the Dominion and in the province, that they are desirous of arriving at an agreement to provide the long sought for accommodation. The provincial government has passed an Act,, which is referred to in the resolution, providing to grant a guarantee of the bonds to the extent of $25,000 a mile for the construction of the road if the Dominion government will undertake its operation. That seemed to be a fairly equal distribution of labour. This resolution is to provide that the Railway Department may have power to enter into negotiations for the operations of this railway on its completion under the terms outlined in the provincial legislation. I understand that a company has already offered to undertake the construction , of this line on the terms indicated in the provincial legislation and outlined in this resolution. If the committee will allow me, I have some details, which I propose to give. The line will extend from St. John to Grand Falls to connect with the National Transcontinental a distance of about 207 miles. It will follow the River St. John to Fredericton a distance of 74 miles, and thence go to Woodstock a distance of 62 miles. From that point to a short distance below Andover it leaves the river, going between that and the International boundary line, a distance of 45 miles. Then it is proposed to cross the river going on the eastern side from Andover to Grand Falls, a distance of about 25 miles.
I need not point out that in this section there is a lot of agricultural production. It has been noticed in this House on one or two occasions that the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) takes great interest in potatoes, an interest accounted for by the fact that the section through which this road is to run, including the constituency he represents, is a great producer of potatoes. Last year along that line, there were something like 150,000 barrels carried out of that territory, and carried under conditions which compelled the farmers to draw them from five to fifteen miles. After better railway facilities are offered, this production no doubt will be doubled and perhaps trebled or quadrupled.
This matter is not new. It has been discussed already on several occasions when the' subsidies were granted. The necessity for the line is acknowledged by everybody, but the question is how to work the line practically. It is proposed that the government should have power to enter into an agreement to operate this line, retaining sixty per cent and handing over forty per cent to the provincial government or the company. It is assumed that a certain standard of road will be required. That standard is outlined in the resolution as the general standard of the National Transcontinental through New Brunswick. That might mean a great deal and it might not mean very much. One part of New Brunswick might be very difficult for railway construction and another very easy. At one point I believe the construction of this line will not be very heavy. I am told that surveys have been made recently, and the

estimate runs from $31,000 per mile to $49,000.
Does that include bridges?

Yes. We must lay down some standard, and as this might form part of a through line before many years, it ought to be built to a fairly good standard at least. In the first place we are offering to operate it at sixty per cent of the gross revenue; and in order to keep the cost of operation down to a reasonable point, it is necessary that we should have a fairly good standard of road. I think there will be no difficulty working out that part of the problem. While, owing to physical difficulty, it may be found very expensive to arrive at a very high standard, I think there will be no difficulty in coming to terms for a standard to toe adopted for that particular section. Although there is a grade of four-tenths of one per cent on eastbound and six-tenths of one per cent on westbound trains, it might be necessary to have a grade of one per cent or more than one per cent on some parts of this line. When we say, therefore, the standard of the Transcontinental, it does not mean that we must adhere strictly to a four-tenths of one per cent on the eastbound traffic or six-tenths of one per cent on the westbound, because the physical conditions might make that impracticable if not impossible.
The other point is the initial equipment. It will be necessary to put in the contract something as to initial equipment, but the initial equipment in a road of that kind need not be such an extravagant item. For the first two or three years, the traffic will not be so heavy that it will require an extraordinary amount of Tolling stock, and the company or the government offering to operate it and supplying rolling stock after the initial equipment will come in for -a larger share of expense as the years go by. But the initial equipment-I do not wish to be held to these figures-roughly speaking, will cost probably a quarter of a million dollars. This amount will probably supply all that will be necessary for this line during the first year or two.
There is another point in this connection. There is a road now recently constructed through a territory that ought to produce good traffic. I refer to the Intemtaional railway, which runs from St. John to St. Leonards on the St. John river, twelve miles from Grand Falls. This International line now being completed running from the Intercolonial at Campbellton, will be within twelve miles of the St. John Valley road when completed. It might be assumed that running rights could be secured over this line from the Grand Trunk Pacific for that twelve- miles.	The question
is being considered also of the International railway being operated as Mr. GRAHAM
a . government railway. I am not sure that that will be done; but if it should be, the government railway would have a line from Campbellton through to St. John in addition to the other. The government railway would then have one loop line all around New Brunswick. I am not sure if our New Brunswick friends would consider that as a good thing, but it would be a good thing for the government railways. These are the main features. I am not proposing this as a great money maker, but rather as a means of providing the people of St. John valley with the railway communication for which they have been asking for so many years.

It must be apparent to any one familiar with the facts in connection with these proposals that the adoption of this resolution in the terms here stated will simply amount to a refusal on the part of this government to cooperate with the government of New Brunswick in the effort it is making to provide the people of St. John valley with this much-needed railway. To any one who is not aware of what has occurred, it might be otherwise. A brief recital of the facts, however, will expose the real meaning of this resolution.	_
I need not refer to the great public necessity which exists for and demands the immediate construction of this railway, because that is admitted by the First Minister, the Minister of Railways, the Minister of Public Works and by the unanimous vote of the legislature of New Brunswick. It is sufficient for this discussion to mention the recent agitation which has stirred the people of the St. John River valley from the county of Madawaska to the city of St. John. That agitation broke out spontaneously so soon as it was learned that this government had committed the crime-if I may toe permitted to quote the language used by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) in this connection-of ignoring the claims of St. John valley in connection with the location of the National Transcontinental in New Brunswick, and carrying 'that railway across the province from Grand Falls to Moncton through a wilderness and unsettled country, which the officers of this government in official reports have described as unsuited for agricultural development.	.
That agitation culminated in a large and influential delegation, representing every settlement, town, village and city in the St. John valley, waiting upon the government of the province of New Brunswick in the spring of 1909, and seeking its assis-'arce for the building of a Tailway for the people of the St. John river. That delegation asked the New Brunswick government to undertake to promote legislation

to guarantee bonds to the extent of $25,000 a mile for the construction of this line of railway. It was suggested that, if the government would give its undertaking in that behalf, the Dominion government could be induced to agree to take the road over on completion and operate it as part of the Intercolonial railway system upon the basis of the Dominion government paying forty per cent of the gross earnings as rental of the railway. The premier of the province of New Brunswick, Hon. Mr. Hazen, at once assured the delegation that he and his government were prepared to engage to promote legislation along these lines, and would do so, if the consent of this government could be procured to taking over and operating the road under a long lease upon the terms stated. A delegation shortly afterwards came to Ottawa, I think, on the 16th of April, 1909, and waited upon a committee of the Executive Council, composed of the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid
I.	curier), the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) .and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley). I had the privilege of being present at the hearing of the delegation. I beard the case as it was presented to that subcommittee of the Council, and I heard the Prime Minister's reply. I may say that the principal spokesman on behalf of the application was Mr. J.	H. Barry, K.C., now Mr Justice Barry, of the Supreme Court of New Brunswick. There were other speakers, including Hon. Mr. Fleming, Provincial Secretary of New Brunswick, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and Mr. Foster, president of the Board of Trade of St. John. Others also urged the government to the acceptance of the proposition. The Prime Minister, in replying to that delegation, stated that the government were very much interested in this matter, that they had heard, before the delegation proceeded to Ottawa, of what had taken place in the province of New Brunswick, had considered it to some extent, and had appointed the committee I have already named, for the purpose of receiving the delegation and hearing their representations. He stated that the proposition was a definite proposition which the government would have to consider. He stated, with regard to the subcommittee, that they had themselves, talked the matter over, and intimated that all three, himself, the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Public Works,, .were favourable to the acceptance of the proposition, but that it would be necessary for them to submit the matter to Council. Mt. Barry, in presenting the case, urged upon the government the necessity of a very early reply, setting forth as a reason the fact that the New Brunswick legislature was then nearing prorogation, and if
legislation were to be passed at the session it would he necessary to have the reply at a very early date, within a day or two. In fact it was suggested that the delegation should return with the reply that day. The Prime Minister spoke in very favourable terms, and, while he stated that it was impossible to give a Teply that day, he intimated that a reply would be given within a few days, and went so faT as to suggest that if the delegation could wait over a few days, the reply of the government would be forthcoming. Every member of that delegation returned to the province of New Brunswick, feeling asssured that the decision of the government would he favourable. The people of the province waited patiently for several weeks without any intimation being received from the Dominion government. Not until the 28th of April was a word of any kind received. On that day an intimation came from the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell); the government seems to have chosen that extraordinary medium to communicate with the provincial government with respect to a definite proposition that the provincial government had submitted to them.

Would the hon. gentleman pardon me? My recollection is that the provincial government never, except through the delegation, communicated with
the Dominion government.
The proposition submitted was the proposition of the provincial government, submitted by the delegation of which I have spoken, one of whose members was the provincial secretary.
I believe I am right in saying that the Dominion government never had a communication directly from the provincial government on this subject.

And perhaps, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crocket) would allow me to correct him before he reads the telegram, by saying that that was sent by me not to the provincial government-I never wrote or telegraphed to them in my life-but to J. J. F. Winslow, secretary of the St. John Valley Railway Company, and in reply to a telegram from him.

The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) states that there was no communication between the provincial government and the federal government on this subject. The provincial government's proposition was submitted by the delegation to which I have referred, and in the way in which I have stated.
The hon. gentleman will pardon me again-
Order.

I rise to correct my hon. friend. He says that I stated that no communication passed between the federal government and the provincial government. What I said was that the provincial government had not communicated any proposition to the federal government.

I understood what the Minister of Public Works stated. I have said two or three times that this proposition was the proposition of the provincial government and was communicated to the federal government through the medium of this	delegation,	one of	whosemembers	was the	provincial	secretary, Mr. Fleming. However, this government did not do the provincial government, or the St. John Valley Railway Company, or the delegation, the courtesy to communicate with them in any way from the 16th of April-notwithstanding the statement made by the Prime Minister -until the 28th of April, when the following telegram was received by Mr. Winslow, secretary of the St. John Valley Railway Company, from the hon. member for Car-leton (Mr. Carvell).
Before the Dominion government can give a positive answer, they require information as to details of proposition. They suggest the local government pass legislation authorizing uruarun 1 eo, subject to condition that Dominion government make satisfactory agreement to operate.
Now, the committee will observe the suggestion of the hon. member for Carleton -and I suppose, the suggestion of the Dominion government-communicated to the provincial government in this extraordinary way, through the medium of a private member of the House, a bitter opponent of the provincial government, was that this government required further details. Now, I happened to be present, not only at the hearing of the delegation i,o which I have referred, but at the meeting of the delegation in the Russell House before the case was presented to the committee of Council. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) was present. The mode of procedure was fully discussed by the delegation. The advice of the hon. member for Carleton and of others was asked; and the case was presented precisely as had been advised by the hon. member and others, the hon. member for Carleton himself joining in the presentation of the case.
Notwithstanding the statement of the Prime Minister that this committee was aware before the delegation came here of what had taken place, and had appointed a committee to receive the representations of that delegation, I did not hear the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Railways, or the Prime Minister, ask any member of that delegation one single ques-Mr. PUGSLEY.
tion with respect to standard of construction or anything of that nature. All information was vouchsafed to the committee of council that was asked for by the members of the government at that time, and it was not until April 28, several days after this delegation had been here that information was conveyed to those interested in the construction of this railway, that any further details were required. The legislature at that time had arranged for prorogation on the following day, and the suggestion that the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick should pass legislation before any intimation of any kind was received from the Dominion government as to whether they would entertain this proposition at all, being so crude and thoroughly unreasonable, was, of course, not acted upon. The matter then stood in abeyance six or seven weeks. No further communication was received by the provincial government or the St. John Valley Railway company from this government.
Does my. hon. friend remember the date of the prorogation of the provincial legislature of that year?

The legislature prorogued the day after the message was received, April 29. If the requisite legislation had been passed, the provincial government would not have been in a position to submit a definite proposition to the federal government which, from the reception given to the delegates by the Prime Minister would, I think, you will readily believe, have received most sympathetic consideration. However, that was not done, and the important question now to consider is how best to facilitate the early commencement of this most important undertaking. As if it were necessary that there should be a full meeting of the Dominion cabinet in order to consider the standard of construction of the railway. The Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Railways, had they been so disposed, could, either of them, surely, have conferred with a sub-committee of the New Brunswick government with reference to the 1781
standard of construction of this railway. The suggestion that there should he a full meeting of the cabinet in order to consider a matter of this kind seems to me utterly

Being sincerely desirous of assisting the construction of the railway by every means in my power, I venture to make a personal suggestion for the consideration of your company and that of the provincial government. It is this-that the government make a definite proposition engaging to obtain legislation authorizing the guaranteeing of bonds for such amount as will be necessary to ensure the construction and equipment, of the railway from Grand Falls to St. John on condition that the Dominion government shall agree to operate it as part of the government railway system on a long lease, and to pay to the province 40 per cent of the gross earnings.
The proposition, of course, should contain a description of the character of the road to be built. For instance, as to the grade, which should not exceed four-tenths of 1 per cent; as to the bridges, which should he of steel; the culverts, of masonry; the rails to be at least 80 pounds per yard; and generally, as to the road being up to the standard of a first class trunk line.
You will readily understand that the railway must he built to a high standard with the most favourable grades obtainable, so as to reduce the operating expenses as much as possible, in order to warrant the government asking the approval of parliament of the operation of the road for 60 per cent of the gross earnings in view of the fact that it takes, upon ,an average, all of the earnings of the Intercolonial to pay the operating expenses.
Of course, if the operating lease were made, the Intercolonial would have to engage to keep the roadbed and rolling stock in proper repair and to make necessary renewals from time to time.
I think you will agree with me that the quickest and best wav to arrive at a satisfactory solution of the question is for the provincial government to make a definite proposition along these lines. If the road is operated as part of the government railway system it will become an important branch. Can not the Intercolonial railway run their rolling stock from Moncton on the St. John Valley railway just as easily as they do upon the Canada Eastern railway? I am going to ask that this resolution be altered so that the government of Canada will at least do some little part besides paying the subsidy in the effort that is being made to secure the construction of this line?

Has the attention of the hon. gentleman been called to section 10 of the Act passed by the New Brunswick legislature at the instance of the New Brunswick government?
Before any of the company's bonds shall be guaranteed, the company shall provide in a manner satisfactory to the Lieutenant Governor in Council, by a deposit in money or other sufficient security, or by a deposit of part money and part security, in addition to such mortgage, for the payment of the interest on such bonds during the construction of the said line of railway, and until the same shall have been fully completed and provided with the initial equipment passed and approved by the government engineer.
My attention has been called to it, and I propose calling the attention of the minister to that and other sections of the Act.
What is the meaning of that?

Those were the terms that the Minister of Public Works deemed it to be his duty to insist on as the condition of this government entering into the consideration of this project. I think I have shown that there were conditions, which the minister must have known would have rendered impossible the construction of this railway, but he did not find the New Brunswick government quite so easy as he thought. They pushed the matter to the extent of passing an Act at the last session of the legislature. My friend from Carleton found that the matter was getting so warm in his constituency and the Minister of Public Works found it so warm along the St. John river that it was necessary that something further should be done in the matter. So a letter was procured from the Prime Minister to the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) which my
hon. friend read at a meeting in the constituency of Carleton. The Prime Minister's letter simply stated that he would stand by the specification as prescribed in the letter of the Minister of Public Works, and insist upon the equipment of this road being made by the government of New Brunswick or by the railway company. Then the New Brunswick legislature took that proposal for what it was worth, they had the Act of last session passed in the terms prescribed by this government, except with respect to the rolling stock.
And tied their own hands, did'nt they?

I am going to show that this resolution misquotes the legislation that was passed in New Brunswick, and is an attempt to deceive the members of this House and the people of the province of New Brunswick. Section 11 reads:
No such agreement shall be entered into with any company or corporation for the construction of the said line of railway or for the guaranteeing of the said bonds, and no such bonds or debentures shall be guaranteed, unless and until the parliament of Canada shall enact legislation authorizing the granting of a subsidy in aid of the construction of the said railway, to the amount of not less than $6,400 per mile, and authorizing the entering, by the said government of Canada into an agreement with such company or corporation and with the government of New Brunswick aforesaid, for the leasing of the said line of railway, when completed, with its appurtenances and rolling stock and for the operation, equipment, maintenance, upkeep, and repair by such government of Canada as part of the government railway system of Canada for a period of 99 years and for the payment by the government of Canada to the said province of New Brunswick or the government thereof, each year, during the said term of 99 years of 40 per cent per annum of the gross earnings of said railway.
The committee will observe that the condition as there set out requires an agreement on the part of this government to lease that road for a period of 99 years, not only to lease it upon completion, but to operate, equip, maintain, upkeep and repair. This resolution -which the Minister of Railways has read deliberately omits the word ' equipment ' and is a false statement of the legislation as passed by the legislature of the province of New Brunswick. It is simply impossible that the construction of this road can be advanced if this legislation passtes the House in its present form, because the government of New Brunswick has prescribed as one of the conditions of the guarantee that" there must be an agreement for the leasing and for the equipment and operation of the railway.
It says maintenance, operation, upkeep and repair.

There is another section No. 16 setting forth the specification in the terms of the minister's letter. That section concludes with this proviso:
And such contracts

That is the contract for the construction and operation of the road.
Provided that such railways shall he equipped by the said company or by the government of Canada with proper and sufficient rolling stock.
So there can be no question as to what the position of the New Brunswick government was upon this matter. Then Mr. Hazen in his speech in the House in introducing this legislation stated that it was most unfair to call upon the province of New Brunswick not only to guarantee bonds to the extent of $25,000 a mile for the construction of the line, but to insist that it should equip this road with rolling stock for operation by the Intercolonial railway. The position of the government was made clear in that respect. Yet this legislation, which purports to be an acceptance of this proposition, is actually a rejection of the offer of the New Brunswick government as embodied in fhat legislation. I am going to move, therefore, Mr. Chairman, that the resolution be amended, and I cannot see what possible objection can be made by any member of this government to the insertion of a word in the preamble of this resolution which will convert it from an untruthful into a truthful preamble. I am going to move:
That the proposed resolution be amended by inserting the word 'equipment' between the words 'operation' and 'maintenance' in the fifteenth line of the preamble and by striking out the words ' with its appurtenances and rolling stock when completed and equipped with rolling stock and for the operation' in the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh lines and substituting in lieu therefor the words, 'when completed with its appurtenances and rolling stock and for the operation and equipment.'
So that the resolution will truthfully set forth the legislation passed by the New Brunswick legislature and conform to the provisions of the New Brunswick Act.
Does my hon. friend think it possible, in view of section 10 of their Act, which says in so many words that they will not guarantee the bonds unless the company provide the initial equipment
They cannot guarantee the bonds.

They cannot guarantee them now under the Act. Does not my hon. friend think that he will be absolutely Mr. CROCKET.
preventing this government from doing anything if he introduces these words?
I have read section 11 of this Act.
Read section 10.

Section 11 of this Act contains the condition set forth in the resolution before the House, and I ask any member of this committee to follow the reading of the preamble of this resolution with the reading of this section.
Read section 10, which provides for guaranteeing the bonds.
It simply nullifies the whole thing if you do that.
This is section 11.
Read section 10.

No such agreement shall be entered into with any company or corporation for the construction of the said line of railway or for the guaranteeing of the said bonds, and no snch bonds or debentures shall be guaranteed unless and until the parliament of Canada shall enact legislation authorizing the granting of a subsidy in aid of the construction of the said railway-

that has already been done.
-to the amount of not less than $6,400 per mile, and authorizing the entering by the said government of Canada into an agreement with such company or corporation and with the government of New Brunswick aforesaid, for the leasing of the said line of railway, when completed, with its appurtenances and rolling stock and for the operation, equipment, maintenance, upkeep and repair-
Does not that provide-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

How can the government of New Brunswick under that legislation guarantee the bonds of this company unless that agreement is entered into with this government under the terms which are there stated, one of the terms being that the government shall undertake to enter into this lease and provide for the operation and equipment of the railway? The preamble states the conditions untruthfully and insists that the government will take it over only when the road is equipped with Tolling stock, which is contrary to the terms of the New Brunswick legislation.
Will my_ hon. friend allow me to ask him a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has intimated that he wishes to close before six o'clock.
I think that I have been pretty indulgent to the Minister ,of Public Works this afternoon.
All right.

I propose, therefore, to move the amendment which I have already read that the word ' equipment5 be inserted in that way, and that the other words that I have read be substituted for the words that appear in lines 26 and 27. Then that resolution will conform precisely with the legislation as it has been passed by the New Brunswick legislature. If the government do not accept that legislation then the whole matter is off, because the legislation of this parliament and the legislation of New Brunswick are at variance, and no work can be gone on with. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel) seconds the motion.

I am quite sure that the words of the resolution which provide that the government shall maintain, operate and keep up tike railway under this lease for ninety-nine years means the providing of the necessary equipment. All that has to be provided by the company is the ini tial equipment. My hon. friend has called attention to section 10 of the New Brunswick Act and also to section 11. I say they both provide very clearly that the company must provide the initial equipment. If the company does not do that the provincial government cannot guarantee the bonds. Take section 10. which provides that:
Before any of the company's bonds shall be guaranteed, the company shall provide, in a manner satisfactory to the Lieutenant Governor in Council, by a deposit in money or other sufficient security, or of a deposit of part money and part security, in addition to such mortgage, for the payment of interest on such bonds during the construction of the said line of railway, and until the same shall have been fully completed and provided with the initial equipment passed and approved by the government engineer.
When that condition is fulfilled, and not until then, has . the provincial government any power to guarantee the bonds, and, Sir, these are the words, not of this government, not of the member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), or myself, but they are the words of the government of New Brunswick which they have introduced into the, statute and asked the legislature to enact. Then, section 11, which my hon. friend relied upon, provides that:
No such agreement, shall be entered into with any company or corporation for the construction of the said line of railway for the guaranteeing of the said bonds, and no such bonds or debentures shall be guaranteed unless and until the parliament of Canada shall enact legislation authorizing the granting of a subsidy in aid of the construction of the said railway to the amount of not less than $6,400 per mile, and authorizing the entering, by the said government of Canada into an agreement with such company or corporation and with the government of New Brunswick aforesaid, for the leasing of the said line of railway when completed with its appurtenances and rolling stock-
Read the next word.
So, Sir, the legislature has provided
They have tied it up.

They have tied their hands. Perhaps they did it because they thought they would prevent the government operation of this St. John Valley railway, which is the last thing in the world th^t the government of New Brunswick wants.
Does not this resolution omit the word ' equipment ' from the preamble?
That is not the point. We are speaking now of the initial equipment.

Is not the condition set forth in the preamble of the resolution taken from section 11, and is not the word ' equipment ' omitted?
Mr. PUGSLEY No, it provides in the first place just as the legislature of New Brunswick, at the instance of the provincial government, has provided: that the company must provide the initial equipment. Then, when the initial equipment is provided the company becomes the lessee; it agrees to operate the road for 99 years, and after the initial equipment is once provided by the company the company has nothing more to do with it. The company must provide the initial rolling stock and the government must provide for the upkeep of the road and the rolling stock during the whole term of 99 years.
Then, what is the object of omitting the word 'equipment?5
There is no object.
Then why not accept the amendment?

The thing is so plain that any man who wishes to understand it can understand it. What the government ask the company to do is to provide for the initial equipment. My hon. friend says it is unfair for this government to require the company to provide the initial equipment, but .the provincial government is requiring the same thing. The provincial government has tied its hands and provided by statute that it cannot guarantee one of these bonds until the company provides the initial equipment, and then it is the railway and the rolling stocK which are to be leased to the government of Canada. Whatever rolling stock the government of Canada puts on the road after the initial equipment is its own rolling stock, but section II provides that the company is to

lease its rolling stock with the road to the government, and that is of course the initial rolling stock which is to be provided by the company. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Crocket) said that the provincial legislature has required certain things, and has excused itself for making these stipulations because of a letter which I wrote to the president of the railway company and which was afterwards confirmed by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. But, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crocket) should have called attention to the fact that in the letter which I wrote to the president of the company I stated that if these terms cannot be agreed upon by the provincial government, then a conference should be held and a modification considered. I held out a hand to the provincial government and gave them an opportunity to say that if they thought these terms too onerous, if they thought it would not be possible to get the company to build and provide the initial equipment for the road, then let them come to the federal government and suggest such modifications as they might require. I have here a letter which I addressed to Mr. Chestnut, who was the president of the railway company, and 1 have a letter which Mr. Chestnut addressed to Mr. Hazen, premier of New Brunswick, in which he referred to an interview he had with me, and in which I told him that if the provincial government regarded these conditions as too hard, then the proper thing for the provincial government to do was to ask the legislature to provide that the specifications and conditions should be left to the Lieutenant Governor in Council. -1 left a way open there for negotiations, and after recess I will read that letter. The provincial government was so anxious to prevent government operation of the St. John Valley railway that they had asked the legislature to absolutely tie their hands so that no matter what modification the Minister of Railways might be willing to make, no matter what change in the situation he might be willing to agree to, the provincial government would not be able to act. It is the most extraordinary action I ever knew a government to take, they being one party to a proposed bargain, we being another, and we suggesting certain terms, they declined to ask the legislature to leave it to them to negotiate; they declined to ask the legislature to allow reconsideration of the conditions, but they asked the legislature to tie their hands so that unless the conditions were complied with in the minutest particular they could not guarantee the bonds. But, Sir, they will be obliged, if they want this road built (as they know now from the report of their own engineer), they will be obliged to go back to the legislature and ask that modifications be enacted, or they will never get a road such as the people of the province of Mr. PUGSLET.
New Brunswick are demanding, and which is necessary for the progress, prosperity and development of that beautiful St. John river valley.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Before recess I was speaking of the equipment of this railway. T would like to understand clearly what my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) desires by his amendment. Is it that, it may be made more clear that the Intercolonial railway is to provide for all equipment after the initial equipment?

I expect my hon. friend from York, to be here in a moment; but I understand that in wishing to insert the word * equipment ' in the resolution, his idea is that it will then devolve upon the Intercolonial railway to provide the rolling stock and to operate the railway after its construction.

If that is what my hon. friend desires by the amendment, I may say that the provincial statute will not permit that to be done. But that, as I understand, was not the substance of the amendment. I understood that he wanted it to appear clearly by the resolution that after the initial equipment, which will probably cost not more than $1,000 a mile, making the total cost about $200,000, or, as the Minister of Railways said, about $250,000. the Intercolonial railway should be bound to furnish the additional equipment that should be required from time to time. I may say to my hon. friend that that is the intention of the government in using the words, ' operation, maintenance, upkeep and repair.' The Minister of Railways intended that that should include all repairs to the rolling stock, all additions to the Tolling stock, the furnishing of the cars, locomotives and equipment necessary to operate the road during the whole term of the lease. This, of course, would be increased from time to time as the business of the road increased.
What is meant by initial equipment?

To enable it to pass the lieutenant Governor in Council of the province of New Brunswick. Under section 10 of the New Brunswick statute it is provided that before any of the bonds shall be guaranteed, the road shall be fully completed and provided with the initial equipment, and that is to be passed and approved by the government engineer. After that is provided satisfactory to the Lieutenant. Governor of New Brunswick, the In-

tercolonial railway takes charge, operates, and provides all the equipment, all the renewals, all the repairs to the rolling stock and everything, including maintenance, which shall be required during the term of the lease.

The last clause of section 10 is: ' and until the same shall have been fully completed and provided with the initial equipment passed and approved by the government engineer.' Then, the minister lost sight of the last clause of section 16: ' and such contract (for the construction of the railway) shall also provide that such railway shall be equipped by the said company or by the government of Canada with proper and sufficient rolling stock.' So that while section 10 has this provision with respect to equipment, section 16 provides that that must he provided either by the company or by the government of Canada. That is the position of the provincial government. The position of this government, as I understand it, is that the rolling stock must be provided out of the provincial guarantee either by the company or by the provincial government.

No; that the initial rolling stock shall be provided by the company; then, iby the lease to which the Dominion of Canada will be a party, the Intercolonial railway shall provide all the rolling stock which shall be required after that during the whole term of the lease.

The minister will see that the company, having available only the $30,000 provincial guarantee and the federal subsidy, must not only build the road, but equip it if this government does not accept the offer of the New Brunswick government as embodied in thfe statute.

Not necessarily. I understand that they will have available $35,000 of a bond issue, of which $25,000 shall be secured by a first mortgage and $10,000 by a second mortgage; also $6,400 a mile of Dominion subsidy; also capital stock to the amount of $900,000. If they can finance the undertaking, they have plenty of securities to place with capitalists for the purpose of raising the neces-sarv money to provide the initial Tolling stock.
That would require the company to raise at least $2,000,000 of their own funds in addition to the guarantee.

Not at all. I do not see why they could not furnish the initial equipment under such a favourable lease as the Dominion government propose to enter into with them. The provincial government absolutely requires that this initial rolling stock shall be provided by the company, because it has to be provided before the bonds are guaranteed. The provincial government is to guarantee the bonds as each ten miles are finished. The Intercolonial railway is not to begin the operation until certain sections of the road are provided with the initial rolling stock by the company. I was asking my hon. friend what he desired by his amendment.

The purpose of the amendment is to make this resolution conform with section 11 of the New Brunswick Act, which provides that the provincial government can guarantee no bonds until this government agrees to lease the road upon completion, and makes an agreement for its equipment, operation, maintenance, upkeep and repair. This preamble leaves out the word ' equipment,' which is in the New Brunswick Act, and which must be in the agreement before the Lieutenant Governor in Council would have authority under this section to guarantee the bonds. I certainly think that this government ought to undertake to provide the initial equipment.
It is absolutely clear that the provincial Act does not admit that, because it provides that the initial equipment must be furnished before the bonds are guaranteed.

The hon. minister says that the Act will not let him. I can give him the assurance that if this government will undertake to provide the initial equipment and the rolling stock, the New Brunswick Act will be very quickly amended if it is necessary. The New Brunswick legis lature is now in session.

Then the hon. gentleman admits that under the New Brunswick Act, as it now stands, we cannot provide the initial equipment. In that Act the provincial legislature says that they cannot guarantee the bonds unless the company provides the initial equipment. That is the statute we are trying to confirm.
Why leave out the word 'equipment.'

It will conflict, because they say the company will provide the initial equipment, and that the New Brunswick government will only guarantee the bonds on that condition. I am quite willing to amend the resolution so as to provide that after the company has furnished the initial equipment, the lessee will provide all the equipment necessary from that date on. That will hurt no one.

The word ' equipment ' has some meaning as it is in the New Brunswick Act. When you recite

the New Brunswick Act, I do not see the justification for leaving it out.

We do not profess to give the exact words of the Act, but only its effect. Take for instance, section 9. It says:	The guarantee is to be a guarantee bonds secured upon the railway franchise, stations, right of way and all rolling stock.
There would be some rolling stock in connection with the construction of the road.
Not at all, because the construction is done by a contractor.
But there must always be some rolling stock.

Not owned by the company. That would be the contractors' rolling stock. What I asked my hon. friend was to make clear what it was he wanted by his amendment. If he wants the Intercolonial railway to provide the initial rolling stock, I say that that is not contemplated by the provincial statute. I say also it would not be fair. The hon. gentleman has quoted the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company leasing the National Transcontinental railway, and he says that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is required to furnish the rolling stock. So it is, but the government leases its road to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for fifty years at a rental of 3 per cent on the cost and gives the road the seven first years of operation absolutely free of rental.
Longer if they do not make a rental.

Yes, three years longer if they do not earn the rental. Is that the case here? No. From the very day the road is finished, from the time each section is finished, the government is authorized to enter upon its operation and not have it free of rent. No, whether the company's road earns the rent or not, whether the operating expenses are cleared or not, out of the total gross earnings the government is bound to pay to the province of New Brunswick, for the purpose of providing interest on the bonds the very large percentage of 40 per cent of the gross earnings of the road. So far from any criticism being made on this government or myself or on my hon. friend from Carl-eton (Mr. Carvell), and the other Liberal members from New Brunswick, who induced my hon. colleague the Minister of Railways to make this agreement we ought to receive the thanks of every man interested in the construction of the railway along the valley of the St. John. This government only agreed to this liberal arrangement because we realize that -we have in that portion of the province of New Brunswick a section of country Mr. BORDEN (Halifax!.
which, I do not hesitate to say, for richness and- fertility of the soil, for the opportunities it affords for supporting a large population, is not surpassed by any part of the Dominion. It is only because the government felt that that section of country, which had been settled so many years, and was absolutely without railway accommodation, was entitled to that accommodation-it was only because of the, strong feeling which my right hon. friend, the First Minister, and the other members of the government have with respect to the claims of the people of that section, that the government considered itself justified in ^making this most liberal arrangement. To show you that we made a most liberal arrangement, let me say that in Ontario where the Grand Trunk have many lines leased, they have scarcely ever paid more than thirty or thirty-five per cent of the gross earnings. I asked Mr. Hays of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway if, in case an arrangement could be made with the provincial government, his company would undertake to operate the road. He said that they would consider its operation, but only on the basis of spventy per cent and thirty per cent. Here however, we have an agreement by this government undertaking that from the very first day the various sections are open to traffic, the government will pay over the large proportion of forty per cent of the gross earnings. I am almost afraid to mention what is the liability this government is undertaking. It is impossible to state that accurately, but I am rather inclined to the view that in addi-+ ion to the subsidy of $6,400 per mile, the government, during the first five years operation of the St. John Valley road, will be obliged to incur a liability of at least $1,-f'OO.OOO. That means an expenditure for the benefit of the people along the St. John valley of at least $2Q0,000 a year. After five years something will begin to come in, the increased earnings will be large, and no doubt the government will then be able to pay over this amount, and probably sixty per cent will cover all the operating expenses of the railway, but the offeT is a most generous one on the part of this government.
