When it was announced that we had agreed to pay forty per cent of the gross earnings, my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), who was formerly Minister of Railways told me, that he was utterly surprised that we had made such a liberal arrangement. I explained to him that it was only by reason of the great importance of the road, and of the very strong desire the government had to give the people of St. John valley this railway accommodation that we agreed to this most liberal treatment.
I want to go back a little over the history

of this St. John Valley railway. I am not going back beyond the year 1909. The hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket) referred to what took place when I was premier of New Brunswick, and sought to secure the construction of this road through Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann. But that is ancient history. The people of St. John valley have waited so long for this road, they are so vitally interested in securing its early completion that they do not care what any public man of New Brunswick did or said even four years ago. They are tired and sick of political and party squabbles, and to a man they are united in a demand that all political differences shall be sunk, all party spirit voted down, and that all public men of the province shall unite in securing the early construction of this railway. What they want is that we on both sides shall earnestly strive and bring to bear our best judgment and ability in order to secure the early construction of the road. I shall begin, not in 1907, but in 1909, when a delegation composed of the directors and principal stockholders of the St. John Valley railway and other people interested in that line came to Ottawa.
They interviewed my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and a number of his colleagues, of whom I was one. And I remember the president of the company was Mr. C. Fred. Chestnut, then mayor of the city of Fredericton. They submitted their proposal and said that the government of New Brunswick had stated to them through the Premier that that government would be willing to get authority from the legislature to guarantee the bonds to the extent of $25,000 per mile, provided this government would, through the Intercolonial railway, operate the road upon the basis of paying to the company, or to the government of New Brunswick, 40 per cent of the gross earnings. It is true, as stated by my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) that the Prime Minister expressed himself in the most sympathetic manner when they got through their presentation of the case, and stated that his answer would be given to them at as early a date as possible. My hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) says that the Prime Minister stated that this was a definite proposal. I was present, and have to take issue with my hon. friend on that point; and I am satisfied that his memory does not serve him rightly with regard to what took place on that occasion. My hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) was there also. I can only say that I have *no recollection of the Prime Minister having made that statement.
How could he?
And, as my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) says, how could he?

If the minister will allow me-is he not aware that the St.
John ' Telegraph ' contained a report of the proceedings before the government on that occasion, telegraphed from Ottawa by their Ottawa correspondent in the course of which it was stated that the Prime Minister described the proposition as a definite proposition.

All I can say is that I have not seen any such report so far as I now recollect, and I have no recollection of the Prime Minister making the statement attributed to him. And he could not make the statement, because there was no definiteness in the proposition; there was only the broad statement that the provincial government would guarantee bonds at $25,000 a mile, provided the government would agree to operate the road as part of the Intercolonial. Does my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) as a reasonable man, not see that the question of operating and of the percentage which would be paid would, in justice to the people of Canada for whom this government speaks and acts, necessarily be the most important question? Could the government afford to have the road built with rails of 40 pounds to the yard? Could it afford to have the road built with wooden bridges, with curves shorter than are suitable for profitable railroad operation, with grades unsuitable for a first-class road ? Surely, the hon. gentleman must see from his own statement that there was no definiteness whatever in their proposition. This interview took place on the 12th of April, and he said that this government actually waited until the 18th of April before giving a reply-
I see that nothing was done until the 28th of April.

Well, the 28th: That is just sixteen days after the interview. Surely my hon. friend cannot be serious when he suggests that sixteen days was a long time for the government to take to consider a question of such enormous importance as this, one which may involve this country in a liability of at least a million dollars in the first five years of the operation of the road, before the traffic reaches the proportions to which we hope it will grow in the not distant future? I think that every reasonable man will. see that if the government waited sixteen days, that- was not an unduly long time to wait. Now, what took place then? My hon. friend from Carleton, as I understand, in response to a request from the secretary of the company, Mr. Winslow, wired that he had seen the Prime Minister-if I remember correctly-and that the Prime Minister suggested that the provincial government should have legislation passed, and then submit their definite proposition to this government, and the government would be



prepared at a very early day to give them an answer. I understand that, upon that telegram being received, a delegation of the people from the St. John valley waited upon the premier of the province, Mr. Hazen, and he promised to introduce legislation in the session of 1909, leading the people to believe that he was going to introduce the legislation providing for the guarantee. But, at the last moment, he declined to do so, for reasons, as I suppose, best known to himself.
The matter then went over. Later on, a communication was made from the president of the company to me, and I wrote the letter of June 19, 1909, to which my hon. friend has referred. I would ask any hon. member of this House, I would ask the people of New Brunswick, and especially those in the St. John valley, to read that letter and see whether it was a proper letter for me, as Minister of Public Works, to have written. I suggest that a definite proposition should he made:	I
suggest that the road should be built to a high standard-I said in a general way that it should be built up to the standard of the Transcontinental, making it a first-class trunk line; I indicated a four-tenths per cent grade and Tails of 80 pounds to the yard, bridges of steel and the roadbed of a first-class line. I did that because I was not then prepared, and am not now prepared to advocate the countenance by this government of the "ranting of any aid to this road, or entering into any contract with the company which may engage in the construction of the road, which does not provide not merely for a local railway, but for one which, in the future, may be_ part of a Transcontinental line which will bear the traffic of the fertile west to the great port of St. John for shipment to the markets of the old world. That is the ideal I had before me, and that is the reason I was anxious to have the road built to a high standard. In that letter, I suggested that if the provincial government made their proposition and we did not accept it, then I would suggest that a conference he held so that modifications might be agreed upon. The provincial government did not act upon that suggestion, and I desire to say now, and to make a statement, which, I am sure, will strike the House as extraordinary, that -the government of New Brunswick which has professed to be so anxious to secure the construction of this St. John valley railway has never directly communicated with the Prime Minister, the Minister of Railways or myself, the member of the government representing the province of New Brunswick, with regard to its construction: every communication has been made through third parties, either officers of the St. John Valley Railway Company or the members of a Mr. PTTGSLEY.
delegation. Later on, when it came to the winter of 1910, Mr. Chestnut, the president of the St. John Valley Railway Company, who had been taking a very great interest in the line, and had done everything possible to secure its early construction, came to see me in Ottawa. And just a few days ago, I received a letter from Mr. Chestnut which is marked ' personal '. Mr. Chestnut speaks as a man who was mayor of Fredericton. He was, and I believe he is to-day, president of the St. John Valley Railway Company. He, as much at all events as any other man, nas taken a hearty interest in this project. He has been several times to Ottawa with reference to it, and has done everything he could to facilitate the undertaking and secure the construction of the road. And, allow me to say, Mr. Chairman, I go into this matter somewhat in detail, because there is a determined effort on the part of certain public men in the province of New Brunswick-I am afraid on the part of the government for which my hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket) presumes to speak to-night when he ventures to give the assurance to the Minister of Railways that the government will amend its Act upon his suggestion, and on receiving word from him, to place the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and myself and this government in a false position with regard to this matter.
Therefore it is that I venture, even although I may weary the House, to go somewhat into detail in connection with what took place.	.
On March 13 of this year Mr. Chestnut wrote me as follows:
Hon. William Pugsley,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Possibly you may remember that the St. John Valley Railway Company sent me to Ottawa, in February of last year, to see you in connection with the possibility of bringing about a modification of the standard, of the proposed road, which would be acceptable to the provincial government. Also to discuss other matters bearing upon the same project. This, of course, was before Mr. Hazen brought down his legislation.
Let my hon. friend mark that Mr. Chestnut came to Ottawa as the president of this company for the purpose of interviewing me in regard to modifications with reference to the standard, and this was before the provincial government had brought down their legislation of last yeaT. Mr. Chestnut says:
This, of course, was before Mr. Hazen brought down his legislation.
You presented your views to me so frankly, and fairly, that I asked for and obtained, your consent to communicate the substance of my interview with you to Premier Hazen, which I did upon my return to this city.
At Mr. Hazen's request I left with him a

memorandum, setting forth what I understood 3'our views to be, in regard to the points then under discussion.
I am now inclosing herewith a copy of said memorandum with the thought that it may, even at this date, be of some interest to you. Especially so perhaps when it is considered that this information was in Mr. Hazen's hands before his Bill re the St. John Valley Railway (section 16, part 2, fixes the standard) was introduced. Also in view of the fact that the local government press now try to make it appear that the federal government fixed an impossible standard. Which of course is ridiculous.
Yours respectfully,

There is the letter from the President of the St. John Valley Railway Company which was organized by leading citizens from all the counties along the valley of the St. John from almost its upper waters down to the city of St. John.
Can the minister state whether Mr. Chestnut interviewed him at Ottawa before Mr. Carvell read the letter the Prime Minister gave him? I think it was on the 25th of January.
No, this would be after.

This is on February 14, 1910, that he writes to Mr. Hazen. Let me read this letter which Mr. Chestnut, as President of the St. John Valley Railway Company, wrote to Air. Hazen.
February 14, 191*.

Did the minister on that occasion inform Mr. Chestnut that the government would be prepared to modify the conditions as laid down in his letter of June 19, and not to insist on a Transcontinental railway standard?
Mr. PTjGSLEY. Whaf I told Mr. Chestnut was that if the standard was objectionable to the local government, then let the provincial government ask the legislature to pass a law giving them authority to guarantee the bond's, but to leave it to the Governor in Council to determine as to the conditions. That would leave the way open, a>
I explained to him, for negotiations between the two governments. I told him that all this government wanted was to secure the construction of a road up to a high standard. If it was found impossible to do that wo were prepared, as the Minister of Railways had told me, to discuss the subject of modifications. The point I want to make is that on February 15, before Mr. Hazen had brought down the legislation in the provincial legislature, he was informed by Mr. Chestnut, the President of the St. John Valley Railway Company, that I had stated that in order to get over the objection which the premier of the province was making, it would be better that he should ask the legislature to provide in the Act that the specification should be subject to the approval of the Lieutenant Governor in Council. That would leave the matter open.
Did the minister at that time intimate to Mr. Chestnut that the government would be prepared to modify the conditions as laid down in the letter of June 19?

Yes. I said to Air. Chestnut that we had in mind, just as Mr. Chestnut says in his letter, to secure the building of a road up to a high standard, up to the general standard of the Transcontinental railway in New Brunswick , but that if in any part there were physical difficulties which .made it reasonably necessary to depart from that standard, I was sure the Minister of Rail-

ways would give favourable *consideration to any request the provincial government might make.
Anything in writing to that effect?

Nothing in writing, but I have Mr. Chestnut's statement to Mr. Hazen of what I suggested to him and Mr. Chestnut conveyed that information to Mr. Hazen. Although they had that intimation from me, what does the provincial government do? They ask the legislature to pass a law, to be found in the statutes of 1910, consisting of three parts. The first part provides for the making of a survey. That has only been completed and the report filed with the provincial legislature in the last few days. Part 2 provides that the Lieutenant Governor in Council may guarantee the bonds of the railway company up to the amount of $25,000 sp mile, but it provides by section 16 that:
The specifications for said railway and the contract between the Lieutenant Governor in Council and such company, for the building of the same, shall require and call for the construction of a first-class trunk line of railway with grades not to exceed four-tenths of one per cent and to be ironed with steel rails weighing not less than 80 pounds to the yard, and shall provide that the bridges shall be of steel superstructure with substructure of stone or cement, culverts to be of masonry or concrete, being the description of the character of the road as set forth in a letter from the Hon. Wm. Pugsley, Minister of Public Works of the Dominion of Canada, to the secretary of the St. John Valley Railway Company, dated the 19th June, 1909, and approved by Sii Wilfrid Laurier, Prime Minister of Canada, in a letter addressed to Mr. F. B. Car-vell, M.P., dated January 28, 1910, and the said line of railway shall he built up to the before mentioned specifications and standard and shall be constructed subject to the inspection by and shall be built to the satisfaction of the provincial engineer or such other engineer or engineers as the Lieutenant Governor in Council may from time to time appoint to inspect the same.
The point I wish to make is that although I told the president of the St. John Valley Railway Company to say to Mr. Hazen that if they objected to the standard they should leave it to the Lieutenant Governor in Council to decide before entering into a contract to guarantee the bonds, and that he should then come to us and suggest what modifications he desired, but with that knowledge the provincial government asks the legislators not to leave that opportunity to determine afterwards as to the specifications, but to tie their hands, to tie themselves hand and foot so that they could not assist any railway unless it was built up to this very high standard. That, Sir, is the legislation that was brought Mr. PUGSLEY..
down. They provided under it, that the company must give a guarantee for the payment of interest upon the bonds for the whole line of road until the whole line is completed. They imposed upon them the very hardest possible conditions.
And pay it in money too.	.

And Urey had to pay that in money. Then they passed part 3, and part 3 provides for a Toad not up to this high standard, but it provides for_ a road which may have the Intercolonial grades, which may begin at a point on the Canadian Pacific railway up the St. John riveT and which may end at another point on the Canadian Pacific railway, this being simply a connecting link between one point on the Canadian Pacific railway and another point. They provide that it may be an electric road, they do not provide foT any security in so far as the bonds are concerned, except what may Ibe the security of the company itself, and they provide that all they would be obliged to do, in so far as interest is concerned, is to make provision for the payment of interest until certain sections of the Toad are completed.
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, when you find a government having legislation enacted with respect to a road that is to be built up to the high standard, that is to be followed by operation by the Intercolonial railway and therefore with behind it. all the credit that belongs to the government a.nd the people of Canada in connection with the operation of this road, when you find that they impose stricter and harsher conditions upon the company even than they do with respect to the building of what may be termed a second class road as railways' are today, considered, and when you find that it may even be an electric railway, what inference would you draw from their conduct? Would it not be that they were determined, by book or by crook, to prevent Intercolonial operation in the St. John Valley? Would you not infer that they were dcing this in the interest of the Canadian Pacific railway or some electrical company which was desirous of developing electrical energy? That is the inference which everyone must draw. That is the inference which the people in that part of the valley of the St. John are drawing to-day and, having drawn that inference, I believe that when the opportunity comes of expressing their opinion they will express it in no uncertain terms.
Now, as I have said, the provincial government have tied themselves hand and foot in so far as this legislation is concerned in connection with Intercolonial operation, they have refused to ask the legislature to give them power to negotiate, they have

refused to give themselves the power to ask for any modification of the terms, but they have passed the hard and fast, east iron provision that is contained in part 2 of the Act. They themselves appointed an engineer to make a survey, a very competent, a very experienced engineer-Mr. David F. Maxwell. The hon. gentleman has not read Mr. Maxwell's report to the committee. I do not believe that either my hon. friend or the provincial government would have derived much comfort from tire report, because I see that this report, made by a gentleman of their own selection, made by a gentleman whom they themselves had appointed, confirms to the fullest extent, the wisdom- of the course which I and my colleagues took, in insisting that this road should be built up to a high standard. That report shows that a road to the Transcontinental railway standard between Grand Falls and St. John with the exception of a comparatively short distance where -there would be a grade of one per cent, like the single pusher grade -at the Tobique upon the Transcontinental railway, would only cost a little over $3,000 per mile more than the second-class road which the government provided for by part 3 of this statute. In other words, the report of Mr. Maxwell shows that-the people will be able to secure a road having practically all the grades up to the standard of the Transcontinental railway for a little over $3,000 per mile more than they would -have to pay for a second-class road with grades -equal to the grades on the Intercolonial railway as proposed by part 3 of this Act, passed -by the legislature at this last session.
That is on the proposed road to St. John?
Yes.

Is the minister aware chat Mr. Maxwell in his- report states that if connection is made with the Canadian Pacific railway at Westfield or Welsford a transcontinental grade is absolu-e-tly out of the question?

I might say to my hon. friend, and I say it with all sincerity, that in so far as the people of the St. John Valley are concerned, they are determined to have a railway extending right down to the-city of St. John. They are determined that the road shall not be a mere branch, a mere appendage of the Canadian Pacific railway. They want competition and they are clamouring for government ownership and government operation.
The minister, in 1907, provided for connection at West-field and Welsford.

That is true, because that was the suggestion of Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann. But things have -moved a long way ahead since 1907. I have learned a great deal also with regard to- the necessity of extending the Transcontinental railway down the valley of the St. John, more than I knew in 1907, and speaking with the knowledge that I have of the city and the people of St. John and of 'the people along the valley of the St. John and having in view the great developments which have already taken place during the last two or three years and which are going to take place in the near future at the port of St. John, the people of -St. John and the people of the St. John valley will not 'be contented with any line up and do-wn that magnificent valley that is to be a mere branch or appendage of 'the Canadian Pacific railway. _ They want a line that will be f. part of a through Transcontinental railway, that they are determined to have and that they will have unless 'their efforts are thwarted by the provincial government, my hon. friend, and those wh.-may be acting with them. Let me real .what the chief engineer appointed by the provincial government says in this report which were tabled only two or three days ago and which my hon. friend has not thought necessary to favour the House with. Speaking as to the section from Fredericton to St. John he says:
Having in mind the shortest route by which the city of St. John and the great developments for transportation purposes likely to be undertaken at Courtenay bay could he reached, and as in order to reach such point involved the crossing of the St. John river at some point, it was thought desirable to deflect the line here-that is at Evandale-and cross over to the left bank at the head of the 'Mistake/ so called; thence the line crosses Gorham creek and enters the valley of Kingston creek, passing through the village of Kingston, Kings county, to the Kennebecasis river, crossing same near the Gondola Point ferry; thence by the left bank of the latter river through Rothesay, Renforth and Torryburn, and enters the city of St. John at the head of Courtenay bay, a distance from Fredericton of 71 miles, which in final location might be slightly reduced and make the total distance from Grand Falls to St. John, 207 miles, the shortest possible route for a railway line that can be got for a continuous low grade between Grand Falls and the city of St. John.
Then he says:
On the division of this line between Fredericton and St. John, at no point has it been found necessary to rise with a grade to so great an elevation as 100 feet above the sea level in the distance of 71 miles, so that the question of grades here does not seriously affect the cost.
I may say that the line by way of Westfield would -be 85 miles from Fredericton to

St. John or 14 miles longer than the line which the engineer of the provincial government favours. In closing the report Mr. Maxwell says:
Section 37 of the Act authorizes the Lieutenant Governor in Council in case of the construction of this road either under part 2 or part 3 to make provision for running rights over the same or any part thereof, for any through line of railway making connection with the port of St. John or the port of L'Etang, St. Andrews or other port in the county of Charlotte.
Let my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) listen to these words of the chief engineer appointed by his friends the government of New Brunswick to make this survey:
In view of this important provision in the Act it would not be advisable to construct a railway along the valley of the St. John river, and particularly below Woodstock, except as specified in part 2 of the Act

And part 2, as my hon. friend knows, is that which provided for the transcontinental standard.
-as the difference in cost of construction of two lines of railway, one built to the stano ard Transcontinental four-tenths of one per. cent grade and the other built to the standard Intercolonial grade of one per cent, would not be at all proportional to the real value of the respective roads for transportation purposes.
And yet, in the face of the report made by this engineer appointed by the pfio-vincial government, my hon. friend sa^s that because we are insisting on the same standard as that approved by the provincial government's own engineer, we are, therefore, endeavouring to block this undertaking. The engineer goes on:
A glance at the map of eastern Canada and the northern part of file state of Maine showB that only one divide exists between the St. Lawrence and the St. John rivers, and that when that divide or summit has been once overcome, the way to the seaboard for a railway, so far as grades are concerned, is made easy.
The National Transcontinental railway on its way from Quebec city to Moncton has already surmounted this St. Lawrence divide and has entered the watershed of the St. John river before reaching the New Brunswick boundary, and continues to follow the same for some miles east of Grand Falls or until it leaves it and climbs over into the watershed of the Miramichi river by what is known as the pusher grade.
The importance, therefore, of the St. John valley as a road for a great highway cannot be over-estimated, and the proposition to build a railway along it is not merely local, but national in both scope and character, and the time is now within reasonable distance when more than one transcontinental railway entering this valley, either by the National road now building, or by what may be a Mr. PTJGSLEY
shorter route across the state of Maine and making an ocean terminus at St. John, must of necessity traverse some portion of the line now under consideration, as it is the existence of this peculiar physical feature of this country that makes possible a railway of this character, and wliat must eventually make of the port of St. John one of the few great shipping ports of the world.
I need nothing more than the report of their own engineer in which he advises that no other standard but the standard of the National Transcontinental railway shall be adopted down the valley of the St. John, to entirely justify the position we took when we insisted that the road should be built to thart. high standard so that it would be capable of forming a part of a transcontinental line. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Crocket) says that this road cannot be built to the standard of the National Transcontinental railway. Let me call his attention to what Mr. Maxwell says in the summary report published in the ' Gleaner ' which is the accredited organ of ithe provincial government. He says:
Grand Falls via Perry Point to St. John, including all bridges, 210 miles, $9,237,390, equals $43,980 per mile.
Now, what is it going to cost to build from Andover to St. John, not up to this standard, but up to the standard of the Intercolonial? He says:
Andover village via Centreville, Lakeville, Woodstock, Fredericton, Gagetown and Perry Point to St. John, 185 miles (Intercolonial grade), approximate, including all bridges, $7,467,319, equals $40,370 per mile.
Therefore, the only difference per mile of getting a road all the way from the point of connection with the Transcontinental line at Grand Falls down ito the port of St. John, by way of Perry Point, including the bridge across the St. John, another across the Belisle. and another across the Kenne-becasis at Perry Point; the difference between this road built up to that standard, except for.a short distance up in Victoria county, and a road* built according to the inferior standard is only $3,600 per mile. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, if in view_ of what their own engineer says, and in view of the fact that there is only a comparatively small difference in cost, whether or not this government has been wise in insisting upon the road being built up to the standard of the Transcontinental railway? My hon. friend refers to an offer made in 1907 to guarantee the bonds for $15,000 per mile. At that time when I was premier of the province we insisted upon a road which would be first-class and capable of forming a part of a trunk line, but the province to-day has agreed to guarantee bonds for $10,000 per mile more than we agreed to guarantee then and

with that guarantee of $25,000 per mile, and with the Dominion subsidy of $6,400 per mile I say that the people of New Brunswick are entitled to more than a second-class road; they are entitled to a road of a high standard, a road which would be capable of forming part of a transcontinental system. But, we have something more definite than that before the people of New Brunswick. We have a proposition made in clear and express terms by Mr. Thomas Malcolm, on behalf of the Quebec & New Brunswick Railway Company, to enter into a contract with the provincial government provided they will guarantee the bonds as each ten miles are completed. He asks nothing beforehand; he does not ask onq dollar from the provincial government until he has built the road section by section; he does not ask for progress estimates in respect of each section, but he is willing to wait until each section of ten miles is fully completed and its proper proportion of rolling stock installed before he will ask the provincial government to guarantee one cent of the bonds that the legislature has authorized them to guarantee. He offers them to build and equip this road for the guarantee of $25,000 per mile with the addition of the Dominion subsidy of $6,400. My hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) says he does not believe that is a sincere offer. And why does he say so? He says, that Mr. Malcolm should have waited until the provincial government proclaimed the Act. Well, I am unable to see that there is any reason in that, because the Act is upon the statute-books for any one to read, and Mr. Malcolm had the right to presume that when the survey was completed the Act would be proclaimed. Anyhow, the proclamation of the Act would not alter 'its language. But, says the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crocket) Mr. Malcolm did not wait to see the surveys and the reports. Well, I have it from Mr. Malcolm that not only himself but the chief engineer of the International railway went over the St. John Valley route, and an experienced railroad man can tell with reasonable certainty what a line of road would cost. We find that Mackenzie & Mann simply made a flying survey in 1907 and their estimate of cost is substantially the estimate that Mr. Maxwell, the engineer of the provincial government, made after a most careful examination of the route.
My hon. friend says there is another reason, that is, that the offer of Mr. Malcolm was circulated in the province of New Brunswick, and was read publicly by Mr. Tweeddale, the member for the county of Victoria, which he says shows that the offer was not bona fide. Mr. Malcolm has explained that that letter was in no sense private, but that it was a public offer, which could have been and should have
been brought down to the legislature; which the provincial government had no right to conceal from the legislature. That offer was dated the 25th of February, and it was not until three weeks later, or more, that Mr. Tweeddale read a copy of it in the House. Mr. Malcolm has explained how Mr. Tweeddale came to get it. There is an application now pending before thp Railway Committee of this parliament to amend the charter of the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway Company. That Bill is in the hands of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), and Mr. Malcolm thought it would be desirable to show to the committee as a reason for getting the time extended, that the company was prepared to build the St. John Valley road, and he sent a copy of the letter to the hon. member for Carleton. Now, the hon. member for CaTleton had a perfect right, if he chose, to send a copy of a public letter to any member of the provincial legislature, especially on a subject in which the people of New Brunswick are intensely interested. I-t seems to me that there is nothing in that which sheuld impugn the bona tides of Mr. Malcolm. But "my hon. friend says that the charter of the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway Company was granted in 1900, and nothing has been done upon it. My hon. friend did not tell the House that it was only during this last year, a comparatively few months ago, that Mr. Malcolm acquired a controlling interest in this charter; so he has informed me.
He was a member of the original company, was he not?
If he was, he was only nominally so.
I may say that he was, and that his associates were the Hon. Senator Costigan, and a clerk in the post office here, Mr. Bertrand.

At all events, Mr. Malcolm has informed me that he has acquired a controlling interest in the charter. Now, who is Mr. Malcolm? He is a gentleman who has recently constructed, as contractor, the International railway, which is 113 miles in length, extending across the province of New Brunswick from Campbellton at the head of the Bay of Chaleurs to the St. John river at St, Leonards. Everybody who has seen that road will say that it is a first-class road. It is not up to the standard of the Transcontinental railway, but it is, I suppose, up to the standard of the Intercolonial railway.
How much did it cost a mile?
According to the report of the inspecting engineer, it cost $23,737 a mile.
Has the minister the standard of construction of that railway?
No, I have not, but I may say that I have been over the road myself, and it is a first-class road in every respect. The highest grade is one and one-half per cent, but that does not occur very often.

I examined the report of the engineer, and also the contract. The maximum grade is 80 feet to the mile, which is more than one and one-half per cent, the minimum curvature is 10 degrees, and the weight of rails 56 pounds to the yard.

I think my hon. friend is mistaken. I think the 80 feet to the mile refers to the grade coming out of Campbellton; elsewhere it is not more than one and one-half per cent. The government of New Brunswick has asked the legislature for authority to have a railroad built with Intercolonial grades up the valley of the St. John.

I think there must be some mistake about the cost of the International railway, because I find in the preamble of the Act of the New Brunswick legislature it is stated to be $27,339 per mile so that there must have been some misrepresentation at that time or some mistake now on the part of the minister.

I am glad that my hon. friend has called attention to that. That was the estimate of Mr. Collingwood Schrei-ber, the chief engineer, made practically at the commencement of the construction of the road, and I think it is very creditable to Mr. Malcolm that, through his economy, his great experience as a railway builder and his ability to organize his construction gangs, he actually constructed the road for $4,000 a mile less than the estimate of the chief engineer. Engineers allow for all contingencies, such as accidents, unfavourable weather, strikes, and so forth, and when you get an experienced railway contractor, who has a large and efficient plant, and who knows how to handle his men, it is often possible for him to make a great saving, and bring the actual cost below the estimate of the engineers, Mr. E. V. Johnson, the inspecting engineer, in his report of his final inspection of the International railway, says that ' the road has been completed, the track laid and the road fully ballasted with good gravel throughout,' and that ' all structures are of substantial and permanent character, bridges being steel girders on massive concrete substructure.' Then he says:
I have now to report the line as in excellent shape throughout and completed in accordance with the contracts.

This report is dated the 17th of December, 1910. There is also the report of the chief engineer who also makes the statement that ' the railway is completed in accordance with the contracts, and is in excellent condition throughout. Then, I have been favoured with a copy of the report of a gentleman whose name would carry great weight with the hon. member for York, that is; Mr. P. S. Archibald, formerly chief engineer of the Intercolonial railway, who made an inspection of this road.
Does ihe minister agree with me in the weight that should be attached to him?

Mr. Archibald is an experienced and very reliable engineer, and I would place great reliance on his statement. He speaks of the road as a good road. What did my hon. friend say was the weight of the rails of the International railway ?
The contract specifies 56 pounds to the yard.

Yes, but he laid a very much heavier rail than the contract called for. Mr. Archibald's report says that they are steel rails, first class, and 67 pounds to the yard. Then my hon. friend says: But these rails are to be 80 pounds to the yard. So they are, but that will only add about $500 or $600 a mile to the cost. It only means a few additional tons per mile, some 18 tons, as between 67-pound and 80-pound rails. If it should fall to the lot of my hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket) to travel over the International railway he will be astonished at the work done for the money this poad cost, $23,000 per mile. There are rock cuttings, stream diversions by the mile, work of the very hardest character.
You should have given him work on the Transcontinental.

That may be. Some people work on a railway and make money; others work on it and lose money. A great deal depends on the experience and judgment of the contractor, and I am prepared to say that Mr. Malcolm is as experienced, able and reliable a contractor as is to be. found in the Dominion. He built a portion of the Bangor and Aroostook railway, away in the northern part of the state of Maine, which is a marvellous success. He built the Tem-iscouata railway from Edmundston up to' its point of junction with the Intercolonial. He has done railway building on the Canadian Pacific railway in the west. It would be difficult to find a man with larger experience and better judgment as a contractor. He made an offer to build this road; he knows whether he can build it or not.

and he made a straight business offer. He said to Mr. Hazen in his letter:	If you'
will agree to guarantee the bonds- of the road as each ten miles of it are finished, and as that proportion of the equipment is furnished, and if you will comply with the conditions contained in the resolution now; before the committee, I will undertake the construction of this road and its initial equipment. More than that, I will give you security for the payment of interest upon every bond which you guarantee until the various sections are finished and the operation of the road is taken over by the Intercolonial. That surely is a business-like straight offer; and if the provincial government has any desire of securing the construction of a first class road, such as recommended by its own engineer, and of saving the province from that possibly enormous liability which must be incurred unless they accept this agreement which the Minister of Railways is asking from this House authority to enter into, they will accept Mr. Malcolm's offer, re-! quiring from him, of course, all reasonable! conditions, and all reasonable security.
Then my hon. friend says that the offer cannot be bona fide for another reason. It is impossible for Mr. Malcolm to carry it out. But what does he say to the proposition to build a second class road from Andover to the city of St. John which would cost $40,000 per mile, or $15,000 per mile more than the bond guarantee, with no provision for operation, and without having the government of Canada back of the) company so far as the operation is concerned? Then he asks:	What can there
possibly be in this for a company which would enable it to finance a dollar beyond the Dominion subsidy, and the guarantee? I may say that if part 2 had been passed by the legislature as the provincial government sought at first to have it passed, providing that 40 per cent of the earnings should go to the province, even after the interest on the bonds were paid, there would have been nothing in it for the company. Would you believe it that when they introduced the Bill, with part 2 in it. they provided that before the company would be allowed to enter into a contract, they, must pay the cost of surveying, some $20,000, and give security, and that after the road was built and the government began to operate it, every dollar of this 40 per cent would go into the provincial treasury, and the company would not receive a dollar? My hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. CaTvell) knows that my statement is correct. I read the Bill over, and although we were prepared for almost anything on the part of the provincial government in order to prevent the Intercolonial from operating the road, yet we were amazed that any one would have the audacity to submit to
the legislature a proposition of that kind. They asked the company to pay $20,000 cost ofl survey and give security before they could enter into a contract for the con->
struction of the road for which, when it would be operated by the Intercolonial, all the moneys the Intercolonial paid were to go into the purse of the province and the company was never to have the opportunity of getting a single cent. That was changed on the representation of the leader of the opposition who pointed out the utter absurdity and injustice of such a proposal; and now, after the interest on the bonds is paid, whatever surplus there is of the 40 per cent will go into the treasury of the company.	.
Mr. hon. friend asks what that amounts ito. Let me tell him. This road is to traverse a section of country which is more fertile than any traversed by the Intercolonial unless it be some of those valleys like the beautiful Sussex valley and those, magnificent marshes up in the . county of Westmorland and some other parts of New Brunswick. It will traverse a country settled for a hundred years <by thrifty, industrious farmers, with a fertile soil capable of producing many hundredfold beyond what it produces to-day. In my opinion, in the course of a very few years the earnings of that road ought to be as great at all events as those of the Intercolonial. I look forward to a time in the not very distant future when trains of the Grand Trunk Pacific destined for the port of St. John will leave the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific at Grand Falls and come down the valley of the St. John to the terminus to be built at Courtenay bay. Or the road will cross the river at a place called Evan-dale and go down to St. John by Kingston and join the Grand Trunk Railway by a branch from Chipman at 23 miles from St. John, and utilize that part^ in connection with the Transcontinental. 'Does my hon. friend know what the gross earnings of the Intercolonial were to the 31st of March, 1910. They were $6,220 per mile. If, in the course of a few years, the gross earnings of the St. John Valley line reach this sum, the 40 per cent which will be paid over to the province will equal $2,488 per mile. After paying the $1,000 per year interest on the hond guarantee, that will leave a surplus of $1,488 per mile to the company. In other words, the 40 per cent of the gross earnings would pay the four per cent on $60,000 per mile, or on $35,000 per mile over and beyond the interest on the bonds guaranteed by the government. In view of the fact that the Intercolonial will operate this road section by section as completed, I know of no better proposition for capitalists. I do not wonder that Mr. Malcolm and his associates should be willing to risk their money; I do not won-

der that the contractor should be willing to risk his plant and services in order to secure the construction of this road and the benefit which will come to this company in the years to come as the result of this government entering into this long lease for the operation of this road on those favourable terms. Remember that the 40 per cent on the gross earnings is not limited to five, ten or twenty years, but is to last for the long term of 99 years.
No matter how large the earnings may be, during the whole of that period of ninety-nine years, the government is obliged to pay to this company, and the province of New Brunswick, this magnificent percentage of forty per cent on the gross earnings. The company will not spend a dollar upon repairs, to renew the rolling stock, provide new locomotives and cars as they are required, and all the time the company will receive this forty per cent upon the gross earnings. Out of that it will pay $1,000 a mile, leaving whatever surplus there may be towards paying dividends upon any additional securities the company may issue.
Now. I apologize for taking so much of the time of the House. I have done it, as I have said, because of the position taken by certain gentlemen in this matter. This government has gone great lengths, lengths for which there is no precedent so far as this government is concerned, to secure the construction of this road, both by the subsidy of $6,400 a mile, and by the agreement to operate and pay this large percentage of the gross earnings. I should have thought that, instead of being criticised, we should have been thanked by every man who desires to see this important enterprise undertaken. The attempt has been made to make us appear the enemies of the road, because we have insisted upon this high standard. It is a matter of the greatest possible gratification to me that, out of the mouth of the very man, who, of all others, is qualified to speak, and does speak, for the provincial government, our action is justified, he haVing reported that it would not be advisable to build a railway down the valley of the St. John river upon any other standard than the one which we have chosen and insisted upon, and that is the standard of the Transcontinental railway in New Brunswick.

It is not my intention to follow and reply to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) in all the various deviations he has made in discussing the subject before you, Mr. Chairman. He has discussed many things, but I notice that he has had very little to say regarding the amendment before the committee. So far as the [hon. gentdeman has; attempted to show the great need of this railway to the people of St. John, and has spoken in admiring terms of the great fertility and the Mr. PUGSTEW
beauty of that country and its great adaptability for farming and fruit growing, I endorse all he has said, and think with him that it is high time that these people should be supplied with something like proper railway facilities. At present, they have no railway facilities whatever; practically the only transportation they get is in the summer time by means of the St. John river. The question before you has been dealt with quite fully from the point of view of the amendment iby my hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket), and it will not be necessary for me to go over the ground he has so well covered. But the fact is, leaving to one side the legal technicalities and the verbiage thrown around the case this evening, the question simply comes down to this:	Will the government equip this
road with rolling stock or will it not? The Minister of Public Works, in speaking of the initiatory movement in this matter, spoke of the visit of the delegation from New Brunswick to Ottawa and their seeing the government. He stated that a definite proposition had not been made. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) said that the Prime Minister could not possibly have stated) that it was a definite proposition that they had before them. My hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket) stated that he had certainly seen such a report of the remarks of the Prime Minister. The hon. gentleman was entirely right. I have here the report of the statement of the Prime Minister, and I will read it to show that the statement of the Minister of Public Works, like so many of his statements, was not so entirely surrounded as it should have been with that necessary element which we all desire to see in the case in statements made in this House. This is how the Prime Minister is reported in the ' Daily Telegraph ' of St. John, in its issue of April 17. 1909:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier made the reply for the government. He declared emphatically that he was in favour of the construction of a line of railway down the valley of the St. John which he knew as one of the most fertile and most productive valleys of Canada which stood in need of a railway. He declared that the government of which he was the head favoured the construction of railways wherever they were needed in Canada. He thought there was no need for him to argue that point, as the government had shown its policy by the appropriation of generous grants of money for railway building.
He was glad to be able to say that the Dominion government had failed to recognize the claims of the St. John Valley railway, which the delegates were now urging, and that the evidence was that the government last year had placed in the list of railway subsidies provision for a double subsidy for any line of railway which might be built down the valley of the St. John. That subsidy wculd stand and would be given as aid when the line was built. The delegation now came

with a further proposal, that on the province guaranteeing bonds of tihe company which was to build the road, the government should have it operated by the Intercolonial and turn over to the company forty per cent of the gross profits. Sir Wilfrid said that was a proposal of a definite kind which would have to be carefully considered.
This is exactly what my hon. friend from York said-that the Prime Minister had stated that this was a definite proposition that was made.

It is a little different-
' a proposal of a definite kind.1

Is not that a ' definite
proposal '?
It does not say a word about the details, the specifications, standard or anything.

If the minister can see any real difference between the two statements, he can see more in it than I can.
It might be found on consideration that it was the best arrangement or it might be found that there could be a better arrangement . . .
But there is the fact, the Prime Minister received this delegation here, heard their, proposal, assented to it, and received it as a definite proposal on behalf of the provincial government. When the Minister of Public Works made public his ultimatum I can assure you that the people of New Brunswick looked upon it a>s a severe backset to any hopes they might have had of getting that railway built. They looked upon it then and look upon it now as evidence that so far from helping this thing along the minister was doing his best to prevent its accomplishment. He insisted on a standard which was not carried out even upon the National Transcontinental going through the province of New Brunswick. He insisted on a four-tenth per cent grade, which is a higher standard than the National Transcontinental has going through New Brunswick. Yet this was a railway which was to be made part of the Intercolonial, which does not approach that standard, but has grades of 1 per cent and even li per cent on parts of its line. It looks as if the minister had tried to prevent this thing going through, that he insisted on such a high grade for this railway that it became almost impossible to hope for its construction. The matter is well understood in New Brunswick. I saw the other day in the public press a notice of a meeting at Gage-town, in Queens county, on February 27, at which the following resolution was adopted:
First, resolved that the meeting express their gratification and hearty concurrence in the legislation passed last winter providing for the guarantee of bonds to the extent of $25,000 per mile in aid of the construction of
the St. John Valley railway, and express their preference to have the said railway operated by steam and under the management of the Intercolonial railway if possible. If not, then by some substantial railway company, with transcontinental connections.
Second, that the Bill introduced in the federal parliament by the Minister of Railways may be so amended as to provide and guarantee that the Intercolonial railway management will take the road over when completed for the running of trains, and put on their own rolling stock for all purposes required.
Third, that should the local government fail to find a company willing to construct the said railway aided by the bond guarantee and Dominion subsidy, then we would heartily approve of them undertaking the construction of the said railway and completing it ready for the running of trains, beginning its construction and securing its completion within reasonable time.
Fourth, that as citizens of the St. John Valley we desire again to express how keenly we feel the want of transportation facilities, and that we are relying on the good offices of both the provincial and Dominion governments in their united and hearty co-operation to secure to us this much-needed railway.
So far as this meeting is concerned, its views are plainly expressed.
That meeting wanted Intercolonial railway operation.

The resolution speaks for itself. This government has made a proposal to build a railway to Hudson bay, and I presume that road will be constructed at the expense of the Dominion. The Dominion government is a wealthy government. New Brunswick is a small province, as we all know, and the provincial government are very much put to it to find means enough to carry on the ordinary business of a province. The Dominion government will doubtless construct the Hudson Bay ! railway. The province of New Brunswick has given a larger subsidy than it has ever given towards any public undertaking of this kind. The minister has *spoken of the great feritility and value of the valley of the River St. John. It has always suffered from want of railway facili-' ties. It would appear to me that it should be the endeavour of this government to assist the province in every shape and form in the laudable desire it has to build this railway and give this most fertile province of New Brunswick something like the railway facilities to which it is entitled. That is all that the people tljere are asking. The people of New Brunswick are taking a tremendous load upon themselves in offering $25,000 a mile to build this line, and all this amendment asks is a slight change whereby there will be placed in this Act Ihe word * equipment,' so as to carry out the intention of the government of New Brunswick. I think the minister would be

doing the right thing towards the province which he especially represents if he would accept the amendment which has been offered by my hon. friend from York, and arrange it in such a way as that the section will read as amended. It appears to me that we would be doing something which he, as a representative of New Brunswick, ought to be glad to do, and which would certainly facilitate this matter by making the proposal acceptable to the people of New Brunswick. It would show that this government were trying to help this project along all they possibly could. I certainly have very much pleasure in seconding the amendment which my hon. friend on my left (Mr. Crocket) has moved.

In view of the very able and lucid statement of this proposed railway legislation by my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), it will only be necessary for me to spend a very few moments indeed in discussing it. I offer no apology for speaking on this question, because, perhaps, I have been more intimately connected with every move concerning this matter made during the last two years than any other hon. member of the House. I know what is required perhaps more intimately than any other man except possibly the minister himself. I have taken a great interest in it because the road, when constructed, will pass through my country for a distance of about fifty miles, and, having my ideas with regard to the work not only in my constituency but in six or seven other constituencies in New Brunswick, I feel its importance. I am fully justified in doing every thing which reasonably can be done in order to secure the construction of this great work. I shall not weary the House with an historical review of this question, and I am only going to refer to one thing. About two years ago now, a number of meetings were held in different parts of the province to talk the railway up and down the river St. John. This railway has been discussed and talked of and legislated upon for at least 25 years to my own recollection, and I do not know how far back of that. On two occasions work has actually commenced. I think that about 20 years ago work was commenced at Fredericton and five or six miles were graded. Through failure to make the necessary financial arrangements they were unable to proceed. About fifteen years ago another company was organized, and, they commenced construction near Woodstock, they spent about $50,000 at different places and failed there also. The present agitation was started two years ago. A delegation from counties all along the river waited upon Hon. Mr. Hazen at Fredericton on the day before the legislature met in 1909. The night before they met the premier, I received a telegram from a Mr. DANIEL.
gentleman at Woodstock telling me that the premier was going to ask them to go to Ottawa and see what could be done there I wired back telling him what had been done; I told him that a subsidy had been voted during the previous year for a road all the way from Grand Falls to St. John and I cited to him the statute where it would be found. Next day when they met the premier he asked them to give him a fortnight he said: if you will get the federal government to agree to operate this road when constructed, and pay 40 per cent of the gross earnings back to the company or the governpient we will guarantee the bonds to the extent of $25,000 a mile. The result of the proposition was the monster delegation of thirty or forty people from all parts of the country which has been referred to by my hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket) and my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel). Very shortly after the delegation went away the Conservative papers of New Brunswick commenced to harp upon the statement that the premier told the delegation that they had made a definite proposition. I never could understand the object for doing so, I never could see why there was so much importance attached to it. You will find that statement in the letter written by Premier Hazen to Mr. Chestnut. The premier said it was a definite proposition. I was present at the meeting, and I know the whole transaction. Tins' delegation met in a room down in the Russell House, about half past nine in the morning, I was sent for, and when I got down there they were all sitting around the room, and they were having a good straight fight among themselves.
New Brunswicker like?

New Brunswicker like. The whole delegation, with the exception of Hon. Mr. Flemming, who was representing the local government, wanted to ask the government to operate this road from Grand Falls to St. John. The Hon. Mr. Flemming refused to do it, and would not go north from a place called Centreville in Carle-ton because he said it was unfair to compete with the existing line of the Canadian Pacific Tailway, and he would never agree to it unless he could not help it. The situation was such that it -was apparent nothing would be done, and Mr. Flemming immediately telegraphed to Mr. Hazen at Fredericton and got a reply in which he consented to the proposition being made. That is all that took place, the only thing we discussed and the only proposition put before the government was whether or not they would agree to operate the road from Grand Falls to St. John and pay to the government of New Brunswick or the company forty per cent of the gross earnings, operating the road as part of the Intercolonial railway,

We went before the government with that proposition, and the answer was given, I think, almost word for word as read by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel) a few minutes ago from the 'St. John Telegraph.' If he can get any comfort out of it, all right, I find no fault. There could have been no kind of definite proposition except this one as to whether this government would operate the road and pay forty per cent of the gross earnings. Nothing was said about grades, guarantees, steel bridges or iron.
Nothing was asked.

It never got to the point where it could he asked. It would not fce possible to make a definite proposition about the road, .and the Minister of Railways objected because there was not something more definite.
He certainly did not make that objection to the delegation.
He certainly did.
I was there and my recollection is that nothing of the kind' took place.
I made the objection, and I was not very popular for doing so.
I was present too, and I do not believe the premier said what my hen. friend from York says he did.
The ' Telegraph ' says he did.

That is not always right. However, a good many more important things have happened since then. The legislature was in session and a delegation of 25 or 30 of the most determined men I ever saw went to Fredericton and they went so far as to call on the provincial secretary to resign his seat if the government did not put the legislation through that year, and they got that promise, but two days afterwards the legislature prorogued, and there was no Act passed. Then some funny things commenced, and we began to get letters from Mr. Hazen, not through the Minister of Railways, and not through the premier, but through Mr. Chestnut the president of the railway company, which had been created by the legislature for the purpose of building the road.
And the chairman of the delegation that waited on the government.

No doubt, and a perfectly reliable gentleman he is, and a man who is as anxious to have this road built as the Minister of Public Works or myself, and a good deal more anxious than the hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket) and the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel).
You want to monopolize all the sincerity in the province.

No, he did not. My recollection is that the Minister of Public Works stated that until Mr. Hazen was prepared to go into details and state what kind of grades and curvatures he would provide for, there was no necessity for an interview. He invited Mr. H-azen to give something more definite, but Mr. Hazen has never done so. The next step was a letter written by the Minister of Public Works telling Mr. Hazen through Mr. Chestnut that if he thought the standard was too high, he ought to ask the legislature to give him the power to decide on these details, hut in the face of that he deliberately placed on the statute-books of New Brunswick, chapter 6 of the Acts of 1910, which not only does not give him the right to have this road built, and operated by the Intercolonial railway, but actually prohibits him' from doing it. We have section after section which binds Mr. Hazen hand and foot and makes it impossible for him to sign an agreement that can be worked out. And now, my hon. friend's friends in the province of New Brunswick have the effrontery to advertise in every Tory newspaper and on every platform in the province that the Minister of Public Works and myself have 'been deliberately planning and scheming to prevent the construction of this road. A year ago, when at Woodstock, I read Sir Wilfrid Laurier's letter agreeing to operate this road as part of the Intercolonial, and stated that I knew a man who would build the road for the assistance was offered, I was laughed at by every Tory newspaper in New Brunswick. But to-night 1 repeat the statement that the road can be and will be built unless Mr. Hazen and the Tory party of New Brunswick prevent it from being built, and it will be built and operated by the Intercolonial railway, and the people of that section will be getting the railway facilities they have been praying for since I was a boy. In order to show how completely Mr. Hazen and the Tory party of New Brunswick have prevent-
Has the hon. member any doubt but that the subsidy of $6,400 per mile would be payable in this case.
Not a particle. But owing to the manner in which Mr. Hazen has tied himself down he cannot sign the contract until the legislation is changed.
You are getting very technical.

Yes, and I can tell you that if ever there was a piece of technical legislation put through any parliament it was the legislation regarding this railway which was put through the legislature of New Brunswick, because everything was done that human ingenuity could do in Mr. CARVELL.
order to try and prevent having this railroad built and operated as part of the Intercolonial railway. When they made that proposition two years ago, they had no idea that this government would accept it, and there was nobody more surprised than the Tory party of New Brunswick when the Prime Minister's letter was read a year ago, and from that day to this they have never ceased to try to concoct some scheme to make it impossible to carry it out, and to enable them to build a road not up to- the standard of the Transcontinental or even of the Intercolonial railway, tout simply a cheap branch line to be controlled and operated by the Canadian Pacific railway. That is the whole transaction. Why, when we came to Ottawa two years ago to meet the government, the Hon. Mr. Flemming came along, and his whole fight was against building a road through the centre because it would compete with the Canadian Pacific railway. He wired to Mr. Hazen to get his consent. The night before, this same Mr. Flemming travelled all the way from Fredericton to Montreal in a private car of Sir William Van Horne. I do not say that Sir William Van Horne influenced him, but when he got to Ottawa, he was 'the most rabid Canadian Pacific railway man I ever met, and he has continued to be so down to the present time, and that is really at the bottom of the whole transaction. I do not blame the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; they are only following a good business proposition. I blame my hon. friend and his friends in the province of New Brunswick for being willing to barter away the rights of the people of that province in order to give this monstrous, corporation a grasp on that part of the province for all time to come. The people of New Brunswick blame them too, and they will find that the people are not half as innocent or as ignorant as my hon. friend and his friends think they are. That is all I have to say about the historic part oi this matter. My hon. friend wants this committee to adopt an amendment of his. I have applied that amendment to the resolution before the committee, and I want to read it as it would appear if his amendment were adopted. The whole trouble with hon. gentlemen opposite seems to be over the equipment. The morning after the Minister of Railways tabled his notice of motion about a month ago, the St. John 'Standard,' the leading Tory organ of the province, and the Fredericton ' Gleaner,' the next leading Tory organ, came out with identical editorials on this question, and the gravamen of their charge was that the federal government were trying to prevent the construction of this road on account of the equipment, When I read these two articles I could not understand what they meant, and I at once went to the laws which the

Tory government themselves passed, and I found that in -section 10 they deliberately provide:
Before any company's bonds shall be guaranteed, the company shall provide, in a manner satisfactory to the Lieutenant Governor in Council, by a deposit in money or other sufficient security, or of a deposit of part money and part security, in addition to such mortgage, for the payment of interest on such bonds during the construction of the said line of railway, and until the same shall have been fully completed and provided with the initial equipment passed and approved by the government engineer.
I also find that by sections 11 and 16 they provided for equipment; and this thing has been going on ever since in the province of New Brunswick. I am surprised' that -my hon. friends bring it up here in view of what has taken place in the last fortnight. Now, I will read the. enacting part of this resolution, with the amendment as proposed:
Now, therefore, it is expedient that His Excellency the Governor in Council be authorized to enter into a contract with any such railroad company and the government of the province of New Brunswick as aforesaid, for the leasing of the said line of railway when completed, with its appurtenances and rolling stock, and for the operation, equipment, maintenance, upkeep and repair by the said government of Canada, as a part of the government railway system of Canada, for a period of ninety-nine years, and for the payment by the government of Canada to the said province of New Brunswick, or the said company, each year during the said term of ninety-nine years, of the forty per centum per annum of the gross earnings of the said railway, as or in the nature of rental therefor.
Does not that conform precisely with the terms of section 11?
No, it does not.
In what respect does it not?
If you make this amendment, then you will be absolutely out of court, because section 10 says that until the road is equipped the government cannot guarantee.
In what respect does this not conform to section 11?
I will tell my hon. friend frankly that I have not read section 11 very carefully.
"I have.

I will read section 11 :
No such agreement shall be entered into with any company or corporation for the construction of the said line of railway or for the guaranteeing of the said bonds, and no such bonds or debentures shall be guaranteed unless and until the parliament of Canada
shall enact legislation authorizing the granting of a subsidy in aid of the construction of the said railway, to the amount of not less than $6,400 per mile, and authorizing the entering, by the said government, of Canada, into an agreement with such company or corporation and with the government ef New Brunswick aforesaid, for the leasing of the said line of railway when completed with its appurtenances and rolling stock, and for the operation, equipment, maintenance, upkeep and repair by said government of Canada, as part of the government railway system of Canada, for a period of ninety-nine years, and foi the payment by the government of Canada to the said province of Neiv Brunswick or_ government thereof, each year during the said term of ninety-nine years of forty per centum per annum of the gross earnings of the said railway as or in the nature of rental therefor.
Whether the amendment complies with section 11 or not does not make any difference, because section 10 provides that there must be equipment, and without equipment Mr. Hazen cannot sign the contract.

Then the contention of the hon. gentleman, as I understand it, is that the amendment as proposed by the hon. member for York is perfectly consistent with section 11, but section 11 is not consistent with section 10?

That, I think, is pretty logical, and that is only one of the circumstances by which Mr. Hazen and the Conservative party have tried to prevent themselves from being in a position to sign the contract. If there is no equipment, how is there going to be any rolling stock to_be leased to the government, for which section 11 provides? My hon. friend from York this afternoon said: Oh, there will be some rolling stock. If this road is constructed as all other roads are, by contractors, there would not be a wheel of rolling stock when the road is completed. What is the use of all this discussion about rolling stock? My hon. friends ignore the fact that a competent railway man goes to the province of New Brunswick and agrees to build this road and put on the rolling stock. There is nobody asking for this amendment. This parliament will be in session probably two months longer; the legislature of New Brunswick is in session; if Mr. Hazen thinks that is vital to the construction of this road, let him change jiis legislation and put the burden on us to see if we will not before we get through.
Does my hon. friend object to this government providing the initial equipment?

This government has
nothing to do with it. It is a company which is going to build the railway.
Under an agreement on the part of the company that this government is to take it over.

That has nothing to do with it. The hon. gentleman spoke about making the poor government of New Brunswick provide the rolling stock, and he dilated on -the poverty of that government and the richness of this.
I do not remember any remark of that kind.

Every other hon. member does. The poor government of New Brunswick, he said, were forced to provide the rolling stock. But who asked that government to do it? They put it in their own Acts that the company should provide the rolling stock. Take the letter, it has been almost insinuated that something unprofessional, something unfair has taken place, that I gave away something to the leader of the opposition in -the New Brunswick legislature. I have no hesitation in telling the whole story. For three or four weeks there has been a notice on the Order Paper that application was to be made by the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway Company for a renewal of a charter, and that order stands in my name. I noticed frequently two of my hon. friends opposite holding down the front bench in the Railway Committee and wondered what was troubling them because as a rule they do not bother that committee very much. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel) asked me when this Bill was coming up, and I said in the ordinary course. Not long afterwards the hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket) asked me to name a day and he said that he had some amendment to propose. I immediately wired Mr. Malcolm that some of our friends opposite from New Brunswick were opposing the Bill for some reason or other. I met him in Montreal and he gave me this letter, marked copy, and signed by himself, and he told me he had submitted it to Mr. Hazen, and that he had agreed to enter into a contract according to the terms of the resolution of the Minister of Railways now under discussion. I wanted an opportunity to make this letter public before the Railway Committee, and I notified the leader of the opposition in New Brunswick to get copies of all documents in connection with that matter. I did not give a copy of this letter as my object was first to get all the information possible from the New Brunswick government about this proposition. Notice was given in -the local house on the 2nd of March, but the First Minister there gave an evasive answer, stated that there was a good deal of correspondence had with different people, and promised to bring down the papers at some future time. About a week ago I went Mr. CARVELL.
home and gave a copy of the letter to some of the prominent Tories in Woodstock and
I	said to them: That is what your government has to meet, and I want to know what it is going to do about it. A copy of that letter was sent to Mr. Hazen on a Saturday and on Tuesday the leader of the opposition moved that it be brought down. Not receiving the letter, on Wednesday night he made it public. I take full responsibility for its publication. It was not marked ' private
Mr. Hazen says it was.
If the hon. gentleman will produce that letter, he will find it is not marked private.
I read a letter from Mr. Malcolm this afternoon in reply to a letter from Mr. Hazen in which Mr. Malcolm referred to the fact that this letter was marked ' private.'

My hon. friend can take what comfort he likes from that. I am giving him the facts, and if he does not accept my version let him produce the letter to Mr. Hazen. There is no reason why my hon. friend should make any trouble in this House or bother his head at all about this matter because this equipment is not coming out of the poor government of New Brunswick or the federal government but out of the contractor or the company. If Mr. Malcolm is willing to put up the money for the equipment, that is his affair. I do not think the people of New Brunswick will lose much sleep or trouble themselves much about who provides the equipment so long as the equipment is provided and the road operated. Therefore I can see no reason why we should adopt this amendment. All the resolution provides is that this government shall have the right to enter into a contract to operate the road for a period of 99 years, when completed and equipped with the initial rolling stock. It is only a question whether parliament will give the Minister of Railways that power or not. If it does, this government will be in a position to carry out the very thing they have been asked to do. In every letter, every resolution, every discussion from beginning to end, the New Brunswick government have asked the company or somebody else to provide the rolling -stock. If my hon. friends can induce the government of New Brunswick to change their legislation calling on the company to provide rolling stock, we will be in a position to meet them. My hon. friend had better have legislation introduced into the New Brunswick legislature amending the specifications and changing section 16 and section
II	about the subsidy.
Are not those the specifications laid down by the Minister of Public Works and approved by the First Minister?

They follow very closely the specifications set forth in the letter of the Minister of Public Works.
