But a year ago my hon. friends knew that the Minister of Public Works was prepared to reduce those specifications if it was thought necessary. But they hid that letter away and did not make it public, and it never was known until the Minister of Public Works made it known here to-night. It will be a surprise to the people of New Brunswick to learn the true facts.
My hon. friends opposite complain that the standard is too high. All right we will change the specifications. All we want is to have the road built and then have it operated by the Intercolonial, and we are passing legislation to have that brought into effect. It is then for the government of Mr. Hazen to say whether they will change _ their legislation and put themselves in a position to meet us and have the road constructed. If they will change that legislation and comply with this resolution, if they will guarantee those bonds and sign the contract, the road will be in construction inside of a month and built inside of two years.

I shall not go into the historical matter on which my hon friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) have spoken, though the latter promised he would not indulge in anything of the kind. I am afraid, however, that he lapsed very far from his pledge before he got through. He spoke of the shackles imposed by the government of New Brunswick. Well, the only shackles they imposed were due to the fact that they accepted literally the proposition of the Minister of Public Works and the right hon. the First Minister and put that in the form of a statute. They simply accepted the offer made by this government in the very terms in which that offer was made. I do not propose to deal with the question of this private letter. Mr. Hazen and the gentleman who wrote it say it was private. The Minister of Public Works and the hon. member for Carleton say they know better and that it was not. We will let that matter stand as it is. Nor will I deal with the very interesting distinction made by the Minister of Public Works between a ' definite proposal ' and a ' proposal of a definite kind.' We will leave that as it is.

Like Sir Charles Tup-per's statement that he could net understand the man who said he cou.d not understand the difference between 'an offer of 180
unrestricted reciprocity ' and ' unrestricted offer: of reciprocity.'
That is much more clear that the distinction the minister is trying to make to-night.
It always puzzles me.
On which side was the minister then?
On the right side.

Let us come down to the question really before us. The Minister of Public Works has told us ot the fertility of the St. John valley and how important it is that it should be afforded the railway communication which it is due. We all agree to that. We all agree that the progress and development of the St. John valley will be very greatly enhanced by the carrying out of the proposal which is made a matter of controversy tonight. But it is a remarkable thing, it seems to me, that the Minister of Public Works should assure us that the production of that valley would be increased not merely a hundred fold but many hundred fold by the construction of this railway, and yet that he should balk so much at an expenditure of $250,000 for the provision of rolling stock. And it is a remarkable thing that my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) should agree entirely with the very proper view of the Minister of Public Works with respect to the St. John valley, and yet should regard adherence .to the particular form of legislation in vogue in this parliament as of much more importance than the construction of that railway. For that is the argument he seriously put forward-I am assuming that he put it forward seribusly. The government of New Brunswick, he says, have rendered it impossible that the railway should be constructed, because, forsooth, we have been accustomed to enact grants of subsidies in a particular form in this parliament. I think he will see, on reflection, that that is not a very weighty argument.

Then, does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax), propose that this parliament should pass a special Act providing a subsidy of $6,400 a mile for this railway regardless of the cost of construction?

I say that if the road is of the importance attached to it by the Minister of Public Works and the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., parliament may well do that and nobody would be much hurt by it. The hon. member for Carleton himself has said that the road would cost so much that the subsidy to be paid would be $6,400 per mile. Then he calls attention to the nature of the New Brunswick statute which requires a subsidy



to the amount of not less than $6,400 a mile, and says, because some technical and more or less frivolous distinction might be drawn, by reason of the very wording of this section, this road is to remain in abeyance forever.
That is what will happen.

That is what will happen-assuming the hon. gentleman's argument to be correct-unless this parliament is willing to put legislation on the statute-book that will provide $6,400 a mile. Then, so far as I am concerned, 1 am ready and willing to support legislation of that kind. But I may sav, if I am to judge by the utterances of the hon. member for Carleton and the Minister of Public Works, they are not willing to go that far for the purpose of bringing about the construction of this railway in the St. John valley. However, the hon. member, perhaps, can explain himself if he likes in the very peculiar and difficult situation in which he finds himself by reason of his somewhat unguarded utterances in that respect.
But, let us come to the real question. The real question, as my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel) put it very tersely and forcibly is this: Is the government of Canada prepared to spend $250,000, the amount named by the Minister of Railways and Canals, in providinig rolling stock for this railway? It has been pointed out that if you follow the analogy of the Grand Trunk Pacific, the government of Canada should provide the rolling stock for this road. No attempt to meet that argument has been made except by declamation and the somewhat heated and excited utterances of the Minister of Public Works and the member for Carleton. But, apart from that, let us come down to the real aspect of the situation created by the proposal of my hon. friend from York that these resolutions should be amended. I say that the recital contained in the resolution submitted to this committee is an incorrect recital, and I challenge contradiction of that statement. It correctly recites the New Brunswick legislation with the exception of one word, and it leaves out that word 'equipment.' Then, when you come to the enacting part of it, you will find in ' Hansard ' to-morrow that the resolution as proposed to be amended by my hon. friend from York is in exact accordance with the New Brunswick legislation, and that the legislation proposed by the Minister of Railways and Canals is not in accord with that legislation. I make that statement and challenge contradiction, for I have compared the two very carefully. I followed the hon. member for Carleton as closely as I could- not to embarrass him, but that I might un-Mr. BORDEN (Halifax)
derstand his argument-and, if there is anything in his argument, or in that of the Minister of Railways and Canals, it is that section 10 modifies the construction of section 11, and, therefore, the Minister of Railways and Canals was justified in departing, as undoubtedly he did, from the language of section 11 when he framed his resolution. If there is anything in the long and wearisome argument made on that side with respect to this matter it amounts to that and nothing more. I am open to correction or interruption if any hon. gentleman does not agree with me. Let us see if there is any contradiction or inconsistency between section 10 and section 11 taken in conjunction with other parts of the statute.
Section 9,

I have looked at these sections pretty carefully, and I think I understand them as well as one can understand them in the brief time I have been able to spend on them. Section 10 reads:
10. Before any of the company's bonds shall be guaranteed, the company shall provide, in a manner satisfactory to the Lieutenant Governor in Council, by a deposit in money or other sufficient security, or of a deposit of part money and part security, in addition to such mortgage, for the payment of interest on such bonds during the construction of the said line of railway, and until the same shall have been fully completed and provided with the initial equipment passed and approved by the government engineer.
Not a word in that inconsistent with section 11 which has been put on 'Hansard' by the hon. member for Carleton. Section 11 is embodied in the terms of this resolution, if the resolution be amended as proposed by my hon. friend from York. What was* the object of section 10? Simply this, that, inasmuch as the 40 per cent could not ba received by the government of New Brunsi wick until after the road had been completed and was earning the revenue, therefore during the intervening period it was required of this company that some provision should be made for the payment of interest. It is absolutely consistent and not in the least conflicting with a word to be found in section 11. What is the general intention of this statute with regard to the equipment? A great deal of light is shed upon it by reference to the concluding words of section 16.
And such contract shall also provide that such railway shall be equipped by the said company or by the government of Canada, with proper and sufficient rolling stock.
What then is the whole scope of the legislation? In the first place, by section 10 provision must be made during the

period antecedent to the operation of the road for the payment of interest upon the bonds guaranteed by the government of New Brunswick. That is plain and simple.
Do not sections 10, 11 and 16 provide that before the government of New Brunswick can guarantee bonds rolling stock must be provided by somebody?

The government of New Brunswick intended that until rolling stock should be provided provision should be made for the interest on those bonds, a most businesslike proposal from every standpoint. After the road should be equipped with rolling stock and should be in operation, then they looked to the revenue derived from the operation of the road for the reimbursement of the interest payable on the bonds, but until that had been accomplished they insisted by section 10 that provision for the payment of that interest should be made. There is nothing in that provision inconsistent with section 11 or section 16.
Does not that provide that some one must provide rolling stock?

Section 16 left it entirely open as to whether the rolling stock should be provided by the company or the government of Canada, as I understand it. Therefore section 11 very properly uses the word rolling stock, because if the rolling stock had been provided by the company the lease must necessarily carry the rolling stock as well. It was possible under the provision of section 16 that the rolling stock under the contract as eventually agreed to would be provided by the company; therefore it was absolutely necessary in section 11 to use the words rolling stock in connection with the lease, because after the company provides the rolling stock it is not only the road but the rolling stock as well that must be leased with it. It seems to me that if you take sections 10, 11 and 16 and construe them in the ordinary commonsense, businesslike meaning of the words, you have not the slightest difficulty from beginning to end. There is not a word in section 10 that conflicts with section 11, there is not a word in section 11 that conflicts with section 16. Because it is open under section 11 to the possibility that the company may provide the rolling stock, therefore you find in section 11 the provision that the road when leased shall carry any rolling stock with it if that rolling stock shall be provided before-
Why do my friends object to rolling stock being provided?

I am discussing the question as to whether the Minister of Railways has properly recited the legis-1804
lation of the province of New Brunswick? It must be apparent to any one that if this proposal is to be carried out it cannot be carried out by provision of one kind in the legislation of New Brunswick and of a different and inconsistent character in the legislation of this parliament. What I am endeavouring to emphasize is that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket) makes this resolution thoroughly consistent with the New Brunswick legislation, while the resolution proposed by the Minister of Railways is not consistent with the New Brunswick legislation, for the reasons to which I have alluded, and which were dealt with in detail by the hon. member for York.

If my hon. friend is so anxious to have this portion of the resolution conform with the statute of New Brunswick, why does not the member for York go further and ask to amend the resolution as to the question of standard and specifications?
Because, as I understand the situation, there is no need-

There must be an
amendment

The New Brunswick
statute specifies the standard as the Minister of Public Works does, the National Transcontinental grade in New Brunswick.	[DOT]

Does he not admit that if this legislation goes through as proposed to be amended by himself, it is even then necessary for the legislature of New Brunswick to change their legislation before they are empowered to sign the contract? Why does he not try to make the whole thing harmonize?

I do not desire that my hon. friend shall interpose with a controversy with the hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket) who is perfectly well able to take care of himself as my hon. friend knows. I am pointing out to hon. gentlemen opposite, especially to the Prime Minister and the _ Minister of Railways, that their recital is an untrue and incorrect recital. The operative part of their resolution does not follow the operative part of the legislation of New Brunswick, and the road cannot be built unless the legislation of this parliament and the legislation of New Brunswick are made to conform. I challenge the contradiction of the statement that the resolution proposed by the Minister- of Railways and Canals does not conform to the legislation of New Brunswick. Therefore, I send back to hon. gentlemen opposite their own words that their action in this respect may well bear the implication that it is not the bona fide in-

tention of the government of Canada to bring about the completion of this road; otherwise they would see to it that their own legislation is conformable to and consistent with the legislation placed on the statute-book of New Brunswick by (the government of that province for the purpose of bringing about the construction of that road which is a matter of vital interest not only to the valley of the River St. John, but to the entire province of New Brunswick.

I might draw attention to the point of order that the hon. gentleman's motion, if it means what he says it does, involves an additional charge on the revenue of Canada. If it does not mean that it would not mean anything. I find that after being pressed pretty hard by the Minister of Public Works, and the member for Carleton, New Brunswick, in trying to meet what I thought was the desire of the people of New Brunswick to help this railway line, I have got into a hornet's nest. I am not so sure I would have done what I did. for I thought I was acting pretty liberally as the head of the Department of Railways, if I had known that two promineid members of the opposition had intended to obstruct this legislation. I expected to have their hearty support, but they have obstructed it at every point, and my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has also been drawn into the question. Let me point out one thing.

Does the Minister of Railways and Canals state that I have been attempting to obstruct the passage of this resolution? I am surprised to hear a statement of that kind coming from a minister of the Crown.
I will put it in another way.
I have been endeavouring to secure the passage of the resolution in a manner that would bring about the construction of this road and make it conform to the legislation of New Brunswick.

I should not use the word 'obstruct'; in place of it I will use the word 'oppose.' We might as well understand that the legislation of New Brunswick from start to finish implies and states in every paragraph relating to it that the company was to provide some rolling stock and equipment. In every paragraph where it is mentioned it states that. My hon. friend says: No, you supply the equipment, and he pretended to state this afternoon what cannot be found in their statute from start to finish. They demand, not this House, not the Minister of Railways, but the provincial government of New Brunswick, in their statute that the Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
company getting this contract shall provide the initial equipment. I will take some clauses not yet mentioned to show that the New Brunswick government, in every part of this Act, acted upon that assumption. Take clause 27 if you like:
Before any such guarantee shall be given, the payment of the said bonds and interest thereon, shall he secured by a trust mortgage, made and executed by the said company to a trust company, to he approved of by the Lieutenant Governor in Council and covering all the said line of railway and its appurtenances.

That is part 3.
Mr. PUG8LEY. That is the second class.

But the same principle applies to both roads, they were to supply the initial eqtdpment at least and the mortgage in either case, either upon this road, or upon the one horse road, as my hon. friend calls it, was to be secured on the lolling stock in accordance with the Act passed by the legislature of New Brunswick. Let me go back a little further and come to clause 16. I agree with the leader of the opposition; I say in this regard that sections 10 and 11 are not consistent one with the other. I agree with the leader of the opposition to the extent that my argument is largely that. I admit further that I take the responsibility, in so far as I have to, for the use of the word 'equipment' not being in the resolution, because we cannot say in one clause that the company shall provide the initial equipment, and in the very next clause that the government shall do it. Let me proceed a little further. Take clause 16. I shall not put it on 'Hansard ' because it has been read. This clause fully accepts the Transcontinental railway standard, practically the standard outlined in the letter of the Minister of Public Works. The government of New Brunswick accepts that standard, and put it in their statute, Upon what ground does my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) ask this House to say that that standard should not be adopted when the government that he speaks for accept it and make it part of their statute?
My amendment does not ask that the standard be changed.

No, but the hon. gentleman's argument was devoted for an hour to an attack upon this government for adopting a standard that the government of New Brunswick have accepted and have adopted and put in their statute. Then, the matter of the standard is wiped out; theie is no complaint on that ground.
That is because this government insisted upon it.

Well, the government oi New Brunswick does not always take the advice of this government. Clause 16 says:

And sucli contract shall also provide that such railway shall be equipped by the said company or by the government of Canada, with proper and sufficient rolling stock.
That is inconsistent with the whole tenor of the statute? Why? The government of Hew Brunswick say first that the 'initial equipment' must be provided by this company. Compare that with the language in clause 10 which I shall read in a moment. Undoubtedly the government of New Brunswick expected that this government, when we came to operate, would supply any ad ditional rolling stock, but to use the word 'equipment' in that regard unqualifiedly was not proper legislation, it was not consistent. and this House should not pass inconsistent legislation merely to make it conform with what we might consider to be inconsistent in some other legislation.
Mr, BORDEN (Halifax). Suppose we assume that my hon. friend's argument as to the meaning of the word 'equipment' in that respect is correct-I do not agree with him in his contention as to that-but if his argument is correct, is not that the best reason why we should insert that word?
That is my argument why we should not do so.
You require the word 'equipment' in the restricted sense to make it conform with the legislation of New Brunswick.
No.
Certainly.
My hon. friend has forgotten or missed the few words with which I introduced my argument on this point.
No, I have not.

My contention is that the legislation of New Brunswick is inconsistent one clause with the other, and we should not make ours wrong because theirs is wrong. In our legislation we are meeting the desires of the New Brunswick legislature because that is what is in every portion of their statute.
The minister did not get my point.
I do not agree at all that we should make our legislation conform with theirs if theirs is wrong, or inconsistent-I do not mean wrong.
If you purport to recite it you ought to recite it correctly.

We are not purporting to recite it; we are purporting to recite the meaning of it. Before I get through I think I will show my hon. friends that we are anxious to meet that situation, so that there will not be the vestige of an excuse for the government of New Brunswick not guaranteeing these bonds and entering into a contract. I have pointed out what I mean about clause 16. Now I will go back to clause 11:
No srrcli agreement shall be entered into with any company or corporation for the construction of the said line of railway or for the guaranteeing of the said bonds, and no such bonds or debentures shall be guaranteed, unless and until the parliament of Canada shall enact legislation authorizing the granting of a subsidy in aid of the construction of the said railway, to the amount of not less than $6,400 per mile, and authorizing the_ entering, by the said government of Canada into an agreement with such company or corporation and with the government of New Brunswick aforesaid, for the leasing of the said line of railway, when completed

Mark the words;
-with its appurtenances and rolling stock.
If this company were not to provide rolling stock why was it put in clause 11 that they must have that rolling stock or the bonds would not be guaranteed? That meant that the company must first furnish the initial rolling stock. That is what they say in section 10 and that is what was in their mind. They thought that as the business increased the operating company must furnish additional rolling stock. They provide in section 10 for initial equipment and then, in the next clause they provide for equipment which overlaps everything. In clause 10 we find a provision that will carry out their idea of initial equipment by the company and of additional equipment by the government of Canada. I think that no reasonable person could take any other meaning from looking into all the circumstances of the statute. I have read section 11 which says that they contemplated that this company must have rolling stock. Let me look back at section 10 and see if it is not based on the same idea:
Before any of the company's bonds shall be guaranteed, the company shall provide, in a manner satisfactory to the Lieutenant Governor in Council, by a deposit in money or other sufficient security, or of a deposit of part money and part security, in addition to such mortgage, for the payment of interest on such bonds during the construction of the said line of railway, and until the same shall have been fully completed and provided with the initial equipment

It means exactly the same and coincides with the other clause, except that the use of the word ' equipment ' shows that the government had it in their mind that it would be reasonable ito expect 'that the company should supply the initial equipment.

What is there in that which is inconsistent with the idea of the government supplying it. The point

of that is, that until the road is in operation and earning a revenue there must be some provision made for - the payment of interest,

They are going to release this money every ten miles, and consequently the section cannot mean what my hon. friend says it does. What they meant to say undoubtedly, and what we aTe willing to provide for. is that, when the road is completed and the government takes it over, as additional rolling stock is needed the government of Canada will provide it for the increasing trade. I cannot see that their legislation means anything else. To put the word ' equipment ' in in two places and to say in one place the company must supply the initial equipment, and in another to say that the government of Canada must supply the equipment is conflicting. I believe the government of New (Brunswick never intended it to mean anything else than that the initial equipment should be supplied by the company, and the company agrees to accept that. I am, therefore, prepared to agree to an amendment, and I think every reasonable man will accept it, which will cover what I think the government of New Brunswick had in its mind and will be what I believe to be reasonable, and that is to add after the word ' operation ' in line 16, the words: ' Including the supply of additional rolling stock from time to time sufficient to handle the traffic as it may increase.' That means that the government of Canada in leasing this road shall agree to supply additional 'rolling stock from time *to time sufficient to meet the needs of the traffic. Surely that would make it plain, and be fair, and it will I believe place in this resolution exactly what I believe the New Brunswick government had in its mind.

The meaning of the legislature can only be found in the construction of the language used, and in my opinion it is utterly impossible to get any such meaning out of section 10 as that which the Minister of Railways has placed upon it. It is perfectly consistent with section 10 either that the equipment shall be supplied by the company or the equipment shall be supplied by /the government of Canada.
Would the hon. gentleman think it reasonable that the government of New Brunswick should suppose that this government would supply the equipment as the road is being constructed?

I am not dealing with suppositions. I am dealing with the language of the statute. There is not one word in section 10 inconsistent with the provision in section 16, that the road may be equipped either by the company or Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
by the government of Canada with proper and sufficient rolling stock.
What does the hon. gentleman make of section 9 which provides that the company shall give a mortgage upon its railway and rolling stock to secure the bonds which the province is to guarantee?

I would not wonder at the Minister of Railways who has not had the advantage of a training in the construction of statutes making an argument of that kind, but I am surprised at the Minister of Public Works who is an able and experienced lawyer, making such a suggestion.
You won't answer?

I will answer very quickly, and the answer is that this statute looked to two possibilities in respect to equipment, one possibility was equipment by the company and the other possibility was equipment by the government of Canada, and it was absolutely essential that both in sections 9 and 11 they should include rolling stock.

If the provincial government was in no way concerned in having the company provide the initial equipment why should they expressly provide that the mortgage for their security should cover the rolling stock?
Because if the rolling stock was there it was businesslike to provide that they should have a lien upon it.

Does my hon. friend think that the company would provide that initial equipment just for fun?.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax)? Certainly not; but in the progress of the negotiations the arrangement might have been that the company would provide the rolling stock, or, that the government of Canada would provide the rolling stock, and it was perfectly reasonable and consistent that the term ' rolling stock ' should be used in sections 9 and 11. I should not think that the Minister of Public Works, who is a lawyer of well-known ability and experience, would put forward such an argument seriously. Section 10 had simply one thing in mind, and that was that the province of New Brunswick should have reasonable provision made, before this road was in operation, for the interest upon those bonds, and hence the wording of that section. It was absolutely immaterial, so far as that clause was concerned, in that aspect, whether the equipment should be provided by the company or by the government of Canada. What they were concerned with was chiefly that until the road was in operation and until revenue was being earned from it, some provision should be

made for the payment of the interest on these bonds. The Minister of Public Works would himself have used about the same language as section 10 is couohed in, to meet the same conditions.

I want to point out to my hon. friend from York that the object of the proposed amendment is to meet the contention which is put forth in the province of New Brunswick for the last three or four weeks, to the effect that they could not build this road on account of the little bit of equipment that is required. They say, if you get rid of the equipment, we can do it; but they are not touching the really important parts of this resolution. If my hon. friend were sincere, and wanted to make this conform to the legislation of New Brunswick, he would cut out the whole of the latter part of the resolution, which reads as follows:
Provided, however, that the said contract shall be entered into only upon the condition that the said railway be constructed upon plans and specifications to be approved of by the Governor in Council upon the recommendation of the Minister of Railways and Canals, and shall be up to the general standard of the said National Transcontinental railway through the said province.
Section 11 of the Provincial Act provides that there can be no grade higher than four-tenths of one per cent. As the legislation stands, the government of New Brunswick could not sign a contract for a road with a higher grade than that.
Is that not the general standard of the Transcontinental?

No, it is not. The general standard is four-tenths of one per cent going east and six-tenths going west, where practicable; but if that is not practicable, the grade going west can be as high as one and one-tenth. When Mr. Hazen and his friends passed this legislation, they particularly located the road to run from Grand Falls to Andover, from Andover to Centreville, from Centreville to Lakeville, and from Lakeville to Woodstock. Now, it is a physical impossibility to build a railway between Clearview and Woodstock on a four-tenths grade, except at a cost of probably $100,000 a mile and by lengthening the road 8 or 10 miles. Therefore the government of New Brunswick will be compelled to change its legislation if it hopes to have the road touilt. My hon. friend from. York is not sincere when he says he is moving this amendment to make it conform to the legislation of New Brunswick. He knows that he is not. He is only moving it for election purposes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not in order to question the sincerity of any member of the House.

If the Chairman wants me to withdraw that, I will do so, and I will say that^if my hon. friend is sincere in wishing to change the unimportant part of the legislation, why does he not move to change the important part, and have a vote upon it? He dare not do it,
I will leave the sincerity of my hon. friend and myself in this matter to the electors of the counties of Garleton and York.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask your decision on the point I raised a few moments ago?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point raised, as I understand, is as to the power of this committee to introduce a word which might have the effect of imposing an additional burden on the people.. The resolution has been brought down on the recommendation of the Governor. By it power is given to the government to enter into a contract for the operation, maintenance, upkeep and repair of a certain railway. A part of the proposed amendment is to introduce after the word ' operation,' the word ' equipment.' It would seem to me that this would mean an additional burden on the people, and therefore would come within the rule forbidding a private member moving an amendment or bringing in a motion involving an additional expenditure. But I am willing to hear the opinion of experienced members of the House on the point before ruling.

I am not sure that the rule applies where a resolution has been introduced and an amendment proposed. When a resolution is brought in by the government, it is obviously not incapable of amendment, and I think I have seen authority that it may be extended in such cases.

My view is that the resolution may be amended, but only in the way of reducing the burden on the people, as in Committee of Supply a private member can not move to increase an appropriation, but can move to reduce.

I was quite aware of the rule which precludes a private member from introducing a resolution or amendment which might entail a financial burden on the people; but I do not think that precludes a private member from moving an amendment to a resolution brought down by the ^government even though it may have the'effect of possibly increasing the expenditure. I certainly can recall instances in which amendments of that kind have been moved in this House. For instance, when the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill

was before this House, amendment after amendment was moved to change the route of the railway, adding possibly to the expense that might be entailed. The first part of this amendment seeks to amend the preamble of the resolution. It is simply only for the purpose of converting an untrue preamble or recital into a true preamble or recital. I submit that the amendment is perfectly in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the amendment of the hon. member had been divided into two parts and that down to line 15 stood alone, I presume I could accept it, it being merely a recital, but in the enacting part, lines 26 and 27, it appears to be in a little different position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax), thinks he knows of occasions when a money resolution was amended so as to extend it
I think that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would not contradict my hon. friend, but I have no such recollection. The spirit of the rule is that ho charge shall be laid upon the public except upon the initiative of the Crown, and it would surprise me if precedent could be quoted to the effect that the rule had been extended in the way suggested. It will strike every member of the committee that if the object of the amendment is to extend the charge upon the people, it would certainly be out of order. I have listened all afternoon to this discussion, and would observe to my hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket) that when the resolution provides for the leasing by the government of the road with its ' appurtenances and rolling stock ' in my humble judgment that is the same as ' equipment.' I cannot see any difference.

Have we been sitting here since three o'clock discussing a matter without knowing that it was out of order?-discussing it from three o'clock until 11.20 and the Prime Minister raised no objection before? If we had known that you, Mr. Chairman, intended raising an objection of that kind, it could have been settled at three o'clock this afternoon. You have allowed this
Order.

But the amendment was handed to you this afternoon. Surely you as chairman should know whether it was out of order
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is at liberty to address himself to the point of order. That is the subject before the Chair and not the conduct of the chairman.

But, on the point of order, I have been under the impression that when an amendment is placed in the chairman's hands he should know whether it was in order or not. In that way, we should be prevented from losing hours and hours, perhaps days, in a discussion over a resolution that could not be voted on. In other words, the Prime Minister, who is leading the House, I should think, would have raised the objection at the time, and not allowed the whole day to go by. I think it is the duty of the Prime Minister to have shown us at the start that he intended to raise this objection. There is no doubt that if the Prime Minister says he will withdraw his opposition as to this being out of order, we can take the vote. But, as he has raised the point of order, the vote cannot be taken. There is some object in preventing the vote being taken. I think it is unfair that we should be here all day, and, at a quarter past eleven, the Minister of Railways should raise a point of order simply to escape a vote.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
No authority has been quoted to me to show that the amendment is in order. I have had handed to me by the clerk a ruling of Speaker Kirkpatrick on a subject closely allied to this, and reported in Desjardin's ' Speakers' Decisions:'
Amendment ruled out of order because its effect would have been to increase the burthen on the people beyond that recommended by the Crown.
The House, according to order, resolves itself into a committee to consider certain proposed resolutions respecting the granting of land, or scrip redeemable in land, to the members of the enrolled militia force actively engaged in suppressing the half-breed and Indian outbreak in the Northwest.
The question being proposed, that the said resolutions be now read a second time; Mr. Watson moved in amendment, seconded by Mr. Carey, that all the words after * now ' to the end of the question be left out, and the words ' recommitted to Committee of the Whole House, with power to amend the same by providing that any member of said enrolled militia who has located a homestead and pre-emption shall, in lieu of the grant hereinbefore mentioned, be entitled to get his pre-emption free,' inserted instead thereof.
Objection being taken to the said proposed amendment on the ground that it was in effect increasing the burthen beyond that recommended by the Crown,
Mr. Speaker said: ' That the point of order was well taken, and that the motion in amendment could not be put.'
It appears to me that this is sufficiently close to the present case to be applicable,

and that the spirit of the rule with regard to increasing public burdens without the recommendation of the Crown applies to the proposed amendment.

The authority which I had in mind is to be found in May's 'Parliamentary Practice page 564:
The committee is not bound by the terms of the provisions which the ministers of the Crown have inserted in the Bill; and any member may propose an increase of the grants specified in these clauses, or to extend the application of the provisions of the Bill, whatever may be the cost resulting therefrom, so long as the power conferred by the royal recommendation is not exceeded.
That is the question here.
Acting on this principle, when, in 1812. a committee was considering a message from the Prince Regent, recommending, in general terms, provision to be made for the family of Mr. Spencer Perceval, amendments were permitted for increasing the provision proposed by the minister; and this practice has been supported by rulings from the chair, though, on the last occasion, not without remarks which deserve careful consideration.
I knew I had seen something of the kind. But there are other authorities later in the book which seem to point in the other direction. But what I have read is what I had in mind.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: My ruling would be that the amendment is not in order.

In accordance with your suggestion, Mr. Chairman, I move that the preamble of the resolution be amended by inserting the word ' equipment ' between ' operation ' and ' maintenance ' in the fifteenth line thereof.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am willing to hear any objection on the point of order, if any member desires. It appears to me) that it is in order to make this amendment as being in the preamble, the recital, and not in the enacting part.	.
Amendment agreed to.
I move that between the word ' with ' and the words ' rolling stock ' in the twenty-seventh line the word ' initialled ' be inserted. That conforms absolutely with section 10.
Amendment agreed to.
You would have to get the assent of the Crown to that.
His Excellency, I think, understood this to be the meaning of the resolution. I do not think it will require the consent of the Crown, it is simply to make the meaning plain.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the proposed amendment involves an increase without the consent of the Crown, I would not be prepared to consent to it.
Better go to the telephone.

The operation really means the addition of that rolling stock, but in order not to have a misunderstanding it is better to have this inserted. There is one other amendment, that the figures ' 50 ' in the phrase ' from Fredericton south a distance of 50 miles ' be changed to 40. The reason for this change is that if we leave it at 50 miles it might be that we could not enter into arrangements to operate that section until a bridge was constructed, which might cause delay.	.

Amendments agreed to.
Resolution reported, read the first and second time and agreed to.
Mr. GRAHAM moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 150) to authorize the government of Canada to acquire by lease a certain line of railway in the province of New Brunswick.
On motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, House adjourned at 11.35 p.m.
Tuesday, March 21, 1911.
